title: The Gender Courtroom
contentHtml: This world is just one giant binary gender courtroom. All the infrastructure, language habits, laws and regulations are built on the logic of a boolean gender — black or white, no in-between states, no non-binary, no spectrum. And it is structured the same way as neuro: the routines, the rules, the tolerance for noise, the unspoken social rules (masking) — everything was made by the cisgender and neurotypical "majority" as the default.

title: Counterfeit Pills
contentHtml: Hmm. I tried many channels to buy my medication, even going abroad — but everything I bought was counterfeit (sigh). It cost me around 40,000–50,000 yuan (mainly because going abroad was so expensive). Once, a fake pill sent me to the hospital for a stomach wash. I really hope society can be more accepting and open up more channels for buying our medication.

title: The Kingdom on the Wasteland
contentHtml: We have been judged without cause and without fairness in the social arena; society exiled us to the wilderness, where we are lashed by long winds and battered by storms. So we need to be there for each other, and we need to find a way to put down roots in this soil-less wasteland. Please keep your compassion. Please be strong and brave. Live with pride, cross over despair, pain and death, and build our "kingdom" on the ruins. — Yuehen

title: The History of Fighting to Be Seen
contentHtml:
Let me share some personal reflections. The 21st century really began with 9/11 on 11 September 2001, sharply twisting the dynamics of geopolitics and civilizational conflict. Two main forces — security fragmentation and economic integration — give this century a peculiar character distinct from the 20th. The 20th century was a century of wars and revolutions, where countless oppressed groups — the peasant and worker proletariat, ethnic minorities, the peoples of Asia, Africa and Latin America, women and sexual minorities (of course overlapping) — stepped onto the historical stage to fight for their basic "legitimacy of being seen", roaring out the bitterness of millennia of oppression through militant struggle, achieving the breakthrough from zero to one, and breaking the cages and shackles of the past. The 21st century will be a process of structural reconstruction. Those same oppressed groups still face oppression in its early phase, but their demands and methods differ from the previous century's: what they seek is not the charity of redistribution but universal recognition and acceptance; not the old one or two-element "universal standard", but de-centering and pluralism; and the ways of pursuing these demands are shifting from the political stage and the streets into the subtle details of everyday life. What will happen in this century, as always in history, is a change in the answers to questions like "Who are we?" and "How should we trust each other?".

The millennia of Chinese civilization left each of us and our elders a deep trust in legal authority, elite rule, the spirit of contract, and ideology. But that trust has proven to have big limits in actual life for us and people like us — transgender people and other minorities. The law doesn't necessarily protect the good; the Peng Yu case led to a moral crisis. The self-media era also punctured mainstream media's monopoly over the "interpretive power" of information, while trust in contract and ideology is increasingly challenged by protectionism and tightening geopolitics. Those walking in front see these challenges first, and also touch bewilderment and pain first: the old order is beginning to crumble — still faintly, but perceptibly — while the new order is nowhere in sight. Looking at Chinese history, each of the three previous great trusts took three to five centuries to form; even counting from 1840, it's less than 200 years. This is one of the sources of our pain.

Back to the present. As I said, this is a transitional period. The difficulty of transitions is that the future may be indefinitely far, and even the dawn may not come. In a transition there are those at the front and those at the back. Those in front hold newer, more pluralist ideas, but they are still in their infancy, lacking strength and voice. Those at the back are closer to the past mainstream, so they are backed by everyone who lacks the courage to move forward or doesn't accept more reasonable ideas — giving them great power and discursive authority. The world today resembles a spring in the shape of a pagoda: the back end is massive, and those in front, wanting to move forward, will inevitably be pulled backward. This abstract tug-of-war, in daily life, becomes the fierce arguments between us and our families or other people who don't understand us — or even more intense forms. But the actual disputed question is merely where this spring should sit right now. And this should be common sense: the common sense of mutual inclusion. Violating that common sense leads to a binary opposition between the transgender group and the cisgender group that should never have existed.

Our education and most of our society measure ourselves and others with an external yardstick handed down from our ancestors. They apply it everywhere, using it to attack others — that is their hatefulness. They internalize it in their minds, forgetting what they were supposed to be — that is their tragedy. What we want to do is throw away this harmful yardstick, so everyone accepts the fact that a person need not be measured by any yardstick: that the basic common sense is that a person is an independent human being before being any gender.

But for now, the overall trend is good, moving in a good direction, because the new people are walking toward transcending the labels of the past, toward independence. I didn't notice writing this much. I wonder if I went off-topic. Hope I didn't (o‿∩) — K

title: The Light Is Breaking — Change Is Here
contentHtml: Before senior year of high school I had no transgender feelings or signs whatsoever — a typical cisgender straight boy. Around senior year, I was still a "leftist" online, and I read Engels' The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. The book hit me hard, but unlike other online leftists, after reading it I began to hate men, to hate my own assigned male identity. A gender anxiety I didn't yet recognize began to build, and I wished to become a "revolutionary" woman. So I changed my gender to female on every platform, interacted with online friends as a passing girl, learned about feminism — and it was only through gradually coming to understand LGBTQIA+ that I realized I was, in fact, transgender.

title: There Will Always Be Something Worth Waiting For
contentHtml: Meow meow... My wish is that everyone walks this path safely and soundly, and that we can all stay happy, forever holding each other. I know I'll live well, because there will always be something worth looking forward to in the future... Like seeing in 2029 that asteroid skimming close to Earth; in 2030 that rocket launching from Wenchang toward the Moon; three total solar eclipses in Australia in the 2030s... Like seeing the day I live as a lovely girl myself. So no matter how hard it is right now, I'll do my best to live. I hope everyone can find their own visible thing to look forward to — that way you'll find the drive to live. May I offer the cats a ci poem: the wild geese carry cold frost through the curtain; the moon-holding clouds drift light, new ice still thin; the watery mirror reflects combing and smoothing; think of perfumed powder, bright cosmetics — hard to learn; jade skin so frail, layered over with dragon-silk; leaning in the east wind, a faint-smiling glance, myriads of flowers drown in shame. ♡ —Rain Antares

contentHtml:

Only when safety, dignity, belonging, love, and physical and mental support truly exist can a person have a better choice than continuing to escape and suffer. If the text upsets you, please leave. You deserve to be treated equally and to heal gently.

Reader note: this piece describes self-harm. Acknowledging the harm of the behaviour and understanding why a person relies on it to carry a psychological function are not contradictory. If it touches your wounds, please swipe away now. Go find real safety; please, be gentle with yourself.

My Childhood

I was born in a very remote little village in Henan. It was poor and not open at all — maybe only slightly better than somewhere deep in the mountains, but Henan itself has countless invisible mountains pressing on people's hearts.

When I was little, my parents went out to earn money and left me at my grandparents' place. My grandparents treated me well.

I have to tell you about my grandfather. He looked very old, his face full of the marks of years. He often told me stories from his childhood — stealing melons from other people's fields, catching crickets. I loved listening to his stories. He loved teaching me to read, and whenever I met a character I didn't know, I always asked him...

As a child I liked sitting in the little room at my grandparents' house, watching the hens outside pecking at bugs, watching the sheep quietly grazing. I also liked watching the big phoenix tree in front of the door — the ants climbing on it, the hens straining to fly up it (there was no chicken coop or nest, so every evening the hens would fly up into that phoenix tree and use its thick branches as their bed).

My Family

Both my parents were busy basically all the time, because farming in the village doesn't bring in any income at all. All four elderly people in my family were ill and needed all kinds of medicine, which dragged our finances down badly.

My mother has a terrible temper; when she was angry she would smash and kick things around. But my father is truly a remarkable person — I really admire him. He carried the weight of the whole family. He basically never got angry with my mother and never fought with her; he would just wait for her to vent and then comfort her. So although arguments were common at home, there were rarely any real conflicts.

My mother often took her bottled-up anger out on me — scolding me for this or that, comparing me to other people's kids, saying I was always lying in bed like a useless person, saying: "Such an ungrateful child, how can you be so unfilial?" Anyway, she was very naggy, but after getting used to it I mostly just let it go in one ear and out the other.

My Life

I'd say my living conditions weren't good. I never had a bedroom of my own; I grew up in a house smaller than a public toilet for over ten years, basically always sleeping in the kitchen or on the floor. I never used a shower stall — bathing meant boiling water on a fire and washing in a big iron basin. I never ate any great delicacies; the big banquet feasts at village weddings and funerals were the best food I ever had.

I often had to help with farm work — carrying watermelons, digging sweet potatoes, peeling garlic, drying wheat, fertilizing the corn, and so on. I don't think of myself as hard-working, because I was always slacking off (it was too hot!). My parents often used that as a reason to warn me to study hard — but this kind of life wasn't something I chose!

My Story

In elementary school I had a few playmates, but according to most people, my personality was strange — now that I think about it, it's probably because I was far too introverted! I loved studying niche games — at the time I was really into Minecraft and PVZ — but what's available on a phone is never rich enough, and I envied those streamers who played on PCs. Since elementary school I had dreamed of owning my own computer, but that was obviously a fantasy — with my family's means it was utterly impossible. So I used my father's leftover 16GB Honor phone (my father was scammed by a phone shop; that piece-of-junk phone cost 900 yuan and even calls kept freezing) and researched how to play Java Edition Minecraft on a phone plus all kinds of modded PVZ. That trained my search skills really well.

At 11 (sixth grade) I started puberty. When I saw that part of myself getting hard, I felt a vague, inexplicable disgust. But I didn't pay any attention to it, because at the time I naively really believed the "elementary-to-middle-school exam" was very important (and what good did those practice papers do? My parents bought me so many of them 🙃).

Seventh grade coursework was really simple; I felt no urgency or pressure at all (I only thought it was ridiculous to wake at 5:30 every morning and run half an hour — completely useless). So I had more time to immerse myself in the virtual world. I loved reading manga, then moved from manga to anime, and became a true "otaku" (two-dimensional person). I really liked slice-of-life shows, although that "everyday" was an everyday I could never actually experience. Seeing the cute girls in those shows didn't give me a crush — it was a strange, inexplicable feeling I couldn't articulate. Once, while scrolling Bilibili, I noticed an ad — I remember it looked like blurbs for a bunch of gender-bender novels. After reading it, that strange feeling surged up crazily. I was so curious that I downloaded the app "菠萝包轻小说" (Pineapple Bun Light Novel) and read those web novels; they felt so weird, but I couldn't stop myself from continuing. At the time I really thought I was some kind of pervert.

I would often sneak glances at female classmates, but only envying their long hair, envying their cute hair accessories. I truly didn't know what was wrong with me, but I couldn't help looking. I often drifted off in class, losing myself in fantasy — imagining that by some mysterious reason and accident I turned into a girl, and the life I'd experience after turning into a girl, and such. I had no idea why I thought this way, but I just did.

At 13 (eighth grade), after much deep thought, I told myself this might be a normal puberty phenomenon, probably because my mind and worldview were not yet fully formed — as an adolescent boy, longing for girls was perfectly normal. I used a set of airtight logic to explain everything to myself. But that was completely useless. No matter how I forced or persuaded myself, the feeling never faded. Every day I drifted off in class; I couldn't concentrate on anything, and I couldn't control myself from thinking about those things in my head. I was practically going insane. Even now I think it was almost an obsession. I often gagged from anxiety and unease, but I just thought I had a weak stomach.

I absolutely hated getting erections — a strong discomfort would sweep through my whole body. Normally I wouldn't notice the thing at all, but it just loved to pop up and demand attention. Every erection gave me extreme revulsion and disgust; I wanted to snap it off — as if it wasn't part of my body.

In the second half of eighth grade, the symptoms became worse. I was anxious every day and couldn't sleep; in class I kept drifting off and stopped understanding lessons, so my grades dropped a lot. I only remember being in pain and miserable, not knowing what was wrong with me. I just thought I was a pervert and a mental patient. My set of excuses was completely useless now, because I'd never seen any boy like me — they were all cheerful and lively, while I was becoming more and more wrong.

One weekend I truly couldn't take it anymore — I desperately wanted to cut off what was down there. I hurt myself with scissors and it bled. I'd never seen such a scene and I've always been afraid of blood, so fear took over my mind and I hurriedly cleaned all the blood and tried to stop the bleeding. Luckily it stopped, and my parents never noticed anything odd. After that I felt even worse. I didn't dare try "self-mutilation" again, but that feeling kept tormenting me. Every day, countless times, I fell uncontrollably into fantasy, because fantasy truly let me find a rare bit of comfort and peace in those illusory, beautiful stories.

Once, while looking up things in the browser, I had the random thought: I could search for information to help myself. So I searched directly: "psychological phenomena in puberty", "what are the phenomena of pubertal development". Yes — I was still brainwashing myself. I still thought it was a puberty phenomenon; I truly believed everyone had the same thoughts as me, that everyone felt anxious about their own bodily development. During that period I kept deceiving myself — even though at the time I myself didn't believe puberty could cause this kind of unexplained harm. The result: I found no useful information at all.

Two weeks later, it hit me to search: "Is often fantasizing about becoming another gender a mental illness?" (Why did I love such long, awkward sentences when I was little?) And I found a marketing post about the "yaoniang" (trans women on hormones) group. After reading it I was terrified: why do these people do this like this? Isn't this just being a "shemale"? Even though I was scared, I secretly searched the term "yaoniang" too. This time I found many posts — I learned why they eat "sugar" (take HRT), and saw their side that the world doesn't understand. Comparing with my own experience, I found a lot of real similarities. I wanted to get closer to them, so I joined a "yaoniang" forum I'd found. I saw people sharing their experiences there — their internal struggles, and the joy of their bodies changing. But I was afraid it was an abyss with no return once entered, a drug addiction that could never be quit, so I hid the forum, only daring to peek in late at night when everyone was asleep.

After that I grew fine whiskers and an Adam's apple. I plucked out every single whisker and pressed hard on my Adam's apple to make it disappear, sometimes choking myself until I vomited before stopping. After seeing the effects of the "sugar" those sisters posted, I always wanted to eat some, but I feared "medicine is three-parts poison" — some enormous side effect — and worried what would happen if I was found out, whether I'd eat myself to death, and so on. I didn't dare touch it at all. Long-term anxiety twisted me a bit, and I started trying more extreme methods to make myself "normal": I bought a pile of cheap small blades and began "fighting poison with poison". At first it worked — my attention was completely drawn to the wounds, so basically no more wild fantasies. But after one or two times I realized it was still completely useless. I truly broke down; I had no idea and no understanding of why I had become like this.

In the end, out of options, with the resolve of a "certain death", I decided to use the 100 yuan New Year money I'd secretly saved to buy "sugar". And I really did buy five boxes of domestic Progynova from a dealer (there were tons of scammers on the forum back then — not getting scammed was really great luck)!! But when they arrived I had no idea how to take them, so I joined the QQ group shared on the forum and asked all kinds of questions. A very kind sister helped answer, but then a moderator came, judged me a "kid with skewed values", cursed me out, and kicked me. I could only ask for help inside the forum, but every time I got called "stupid brat" or "dead 郭楠 (Chinese male), stop coming here for attention". I couldn't dare speak anymore, so I secretly rejoined the QQ group and slowly rummaged through the group files myself.

I finally did find a useful document. When I opened and read it, I found it was truly detailed, so I treasured it like a gem — studying it seriously every night, even reviewing parts I'd forgotten. I learned about the effects of various drugs and the damage they might do to the body, and at last I learned what transgender actually means. I immersed myself in it every day, imagining the changes those medicines would bring to my body, feeling inexplicably happy inside. I carried one box of domestic Progynova with me and hid the other four in the deepest part of the cupboard. For nearly a month, the masculine development I hated had stalled. I was thrilled when I noticed, but also felt deeply unsettled: I'm letting my parents down by secretly taking this medicine; what if I become sterile later? What if an outsider finds out and it gets around — how ugly would that be... Yet I couldn't make myself stop, because the effect of those drugs made me feel like I was finally being myself.

One day after school, the moment I got home, my father pulled out four boxes of Progynova and questioned me sternly: "What is this?" I was so scared I stammered, then lied that a girl classmate had thrown them away and I'd taken them to play with. But does anyone believe a lie that cheap? I had no choice but to tell him everything I'd been hiding. He seemed shocked — he said only "I didn't even do this when I was a boy" — and since we both had school the next day, we went to bed early. But neither of us slept a wink.

Later, my father thought I might have depression from the pressure of studying, so he took me to the city's psychiatric hospital. The result: severe depression, and a pile of psychiatric drugs. Every time I took those pills I got dizzy and could barely think; I was afraid of that feeling, so I kept skipping them. Out of options, my father took me to the big Zhengzhou hospital (very "parent-arranged treatment" vibes). I still remember that doctor — although he didn't understand transgender, he was genuinely kind; he helped defuse both our emotions and spoke warmly. In the end, he prescribed a few boxes of sertraline. My father, seeing how poor my state was, applied for a six-month leave of absence from school.

During my leave he kept trying to find out what illness I had. To my surprise, he stumbled on Pan Bailin's videos somehow, and suggested taking me to Peking University Third Hospital. I was truly stunned! But Pan Bailin's appointment was too hard to get, so all we could get was Chang Xu's. After much fussing I got my little certificate (a useless scrap of paper). After that my parents stopped interfering and never brought it up again — but they've always thought I'd get better once I grew up. I hoped so too — I'd really get better. Now it looks like that hope is fading 😖

My Attitude

Truthfully, from the beginning I've been a pessimist, living each day with negative thoughts. I'm not even a good person. I've told the certificate story simply and quickly, but at the very start my parents spent all day making snide remarks — saying I was addicted to the medicine, that any little oddity in me was caused by the medicine! I once held extremely negative thoughts of suicide, but I also hated this world so much that the twisted version of me wanted to drag a few people "as company" to the grave before dying — so I went on X and crazily attacked other trans people. After three days of madness my account was finally banned. Only then did I start reflecting. Before that I also thought: life is this rotten, might as well die. During my leave I lay in bed giving up on everything, doing nothing but scrolling my phone and insulting people. I copied others and started OD-ing as self-harm, knocking myself out of my mind every day — at the time I really was neither human nor ghost. After that reflection I finally saw what I was doing. I sent apology letters to everyone I had attacked and quit the internet. Then I threw away all the medicine and blades — but I still kept the giving-up lifestyle, scrolling videos every day.

Once I ran into a video by the Bilibili uploader Shaxin Chengfen Jiang about surviving as a homeless man, and after reading the comments, I learned that this really is how some people live. I thought: if a person's life has come to this, why not just die? But the optimism that uploader showed — that tenacity of giving everything just to keep living — truly moved me deeply. For the first time I felt that living itself is also magnificent. Early death and late death are both death, so why not keep living and see what tomorrow brings? I never chase grand dreams — I can't achieve them, and there's no need to add extra pressure to myself. Right now I only want to live in each present moment, and fight against this rotten, garbage world to the last second!!! (I'm quite the chuuni 😋)

My Future

The phoenix tree in my grandmother's yard was cut down long ago, yet the old roots still grow new sprouts. Yes — as long as you keep living, you can always put out a new shoot! After wind and rain, not necessarily a rainbow — but the rain always stops, and the sky always clears. The future is like the weather: unpredictable, full of unknowns.

People are the same — like regions of land, each with its own unique climate, yet even so, every region has its own clear day. More or less, keep going and you'll always see it! So keep walking on, strong and steady — let's see what good weather tomorrow brings?

Bits and Pieces

  1. Actually, many times I had the urge to buy women's clothes, but my inferiority complex stopped me every time. I'm probably one of the very rare trans people on nearly three years of HRT who has never once touched a dress 🥲
  2. After I turned 16, while eating "sugar" I basically stopped feeling obvious gender dysphoria; each time I felt like I'd become a normal person, so I tried stopping the meds — but within less than a week, the disgust at masculine development slammed back. Forced to choose, I continued taking them. In the end I just never stopped — staying on them continuously is better for the body than starting and stopping.
  3. I used to be a very introverted person; the change to now really owes a thank-you to a departed sister. She added me in the group and "forcefully" voice-called me. Because of her I really became much livelier — even though she may not have realized it, and we weren't very close. I'm truly grateful to her. May she rest well in heaven 🙏
  4. I used to fiercely deny that I was trans, because several sisters came to "diagnose" me during my self-exploration period; after hearing my story they insisted with certainty that I was trans. Back then I understood nothing and only felt deep fear — thinking they were "brainwashing" me. That produced severe self-transphobia and self-hatred; even today it may not have fully faded...
  5. I originally wanted to write a beautiful preamble or opening, but after thinking about it, it's too brain-draining — and honestly, getting straight to the story is more genuine (we country folk don't fuss about such things 😆)

2026.8.19 Kaifeng

title: Do Everything You Can to Not Forget the Past
contentHtml: For all our kind, the living and the departed: do everything you can to never forget the past, never stop being angry, never give up the struggle, never forgive...

title: Trust Yourself — You'll Reach the End You Aimed For
contentHtml: I think the only reason I can keep on living is that I refuse to bow: why should I live badly? This is not my destiny. Carrying this in my heart, I take on every kind of challenge. I won't believe any label anyone puts on me — whether they call me abnormal, or incapable — those are just their eyes' judgment. I don't accept those shackles. Living in someone else's eyes is the same as handing them your eyes and your brain; it makes you lose direction. In this whole world, only I will always stand on my side — trust myself unconditionally, train myself without pause, take care of myself, love myself. The road ahead is long. Trust that you will reach the end you aimed for.

A classmate at my school, an mtx in the same grade, fell into a suicidal crisis and asked me for help. I agonized over it for a long time, tried my best to talk them out of it, but still failed to persuade them. Then, one after another, both of us acted on self-harm (mine from my own reasons compounded with guilt). We were both rescued, and both forced to take a long leave of absence.

title: Swamped in Troubles, Forced Out of School
contentHtml: I was abandoned by my parents for reasons unrelated to my transgender identity, and these debuffs piled on top of each other... Because I feared the relative who actually raised me — with his outdated views — might refuse to keep raising me after I was "blown out of the closet", I waited until 22 to even start HRT. And all that is nothing compared to the worst part: I can't go back to the big city where I was born to use its educational resources, because schools there don't allow boarding — and being abandoned by my parents leaves me nowhere to live. Also, if I sat the high-school entrance exam in my birthplace, I'd have to sue my parents for child support — but the relative raising me wants to shield one of my biological parents. So I was forced out of school. Sigh...

title: Barely Clinging On — But Picking Up the Paintbrush
contentHtml: Because of severe mental illness that began in early middle school for all kinds of reasons, I barely hung on until university, then dropped out at the end of the first semester! Now I'm working hard to become an outstanding artist — that way I can win more visibility for groups like enby, who have been systematically ignored for so long. Coming out publicly as trans probably means someday I'll hit the glass ceiling, but overall this part is still my own stubborn effort and one of my biggest sources of motivation.

title: The Pain of Being Misgendered
contentHtml: Even though my father is no longer my legal guardian, he still insists on misgendering me — like: "you'll always be my beloved son." I've made it very clear that this makes me uncomfortable, but he keeps saying it anyway. I can only feel pain because of it.

title: The Lives I've Met
contentHtml: I don't have any particularly special experience, but after starting to communicate with my kind, I've met people who started HRT at just over ten years old; people over thirty, nearly forty, still unable to afford SRS; people whose parents supported them wholeheartedly and were truly happy; and people who, because the real-world family and friends never understood them, finally chose to go to death with a calm acceptance. Everyone has their own difficulties, their own life. What I want to say to all my kind: love yourself well, let yourself shine — you will definitely receive the love that belongs to you.

title: Puberty Too Early — I Lost Every Relationship Around Me
contentHtml: I'm very disappointed in myself. Because I developed too early, I lost all the relationships around me.

title: The Fence and the Pushed-Open Door
contentHtml: I was once publicly pantsed in a classroom with both boys and girls present — several boys pinned me down, some holding my arms, some my legs, some pulling down my trousers. I was once showering in the dormitory when someone barged in and loudly commented on my body, and threw the bathroom door wide open, calling other companions over to watch me naked. Afterwards, they told every boy and girl in the class that my naked body had been seen.

title: Love That Sprouted
contentHtml: Honestly, the way I got together with my partner was really wonderful. About a year ago, she confessed her feelings to me. Back then my gender dysphoria was severe and I was very insecure, always feeling I didn't deserve her — I even told her outright that I wanted to become a girl and asked her to give up on me. (I only learned later that she's a lesbian.) But she said to me: "You ARE a cute girl. If you really can't accept being this way right now, I'll keep waiting — until you become who you dream of being." Even though I don't pass at all and am not cute, and I don't know whether her answer was truly sincere — at least I chose to believe it. It was precisely because of her support that I could boldly start HRT. If there's anything to tell my sisters: if someone as ugly, untalented, and dim-witted as me can meet a partner who supports them, then you are all better and harder-working than me, so you will definitely find the love you dream of!

title: Driving Alone Through the Dark Night
contentHtml: I was once held in a detention centre for 37 days after my political comments were defined as "picking quarrels and provoking trouble", and was finally released on bail pending trial. I grew up in a family with no relatives and no support; I held on entirely on my own willpower. So I consider myself a very steadfast, strong person — but in reality I have almost no friends; only my ex-girlfriend keeps accompanying me and understanding me, even though we're a thousand miles apart now. In my heart I still hope to make a few friends — even just to play games together sometimes. I'm writing as the thoughts come, so I'll stop here for now.

title: The Discipline Behind the Fear
contentHtml: I've always had gender identity issues, but my fear of change runs deep — I firmly believe that unless the sex chromosomes change, HRT can only bring me closer to another gender, never truly make me into it. title: The Diagnosis Certificate Nobody Understood
contentHtml: I started HRT on 26.4.12. On 26.7.5 my parents went through my schoolbag and found the HRT drugs. They cursed at me and hit me, and wanted to subject me to conversion therapy. Under my guidance, they took me to Dr. Di Xiaolan, who gave me the transsexualism diagnosis. Despite Dr. Di's persuasion, they refused to take me to Peking University Third Hospital to prescribe HRT, and warned me they'd break my legs if I bought the medication again.

title: Fluid Shapes
contentHtml:
I actually came across the concept of "transgender" quite early, but at the time I didn't explore it deeply. Since childhood I've wished and yearned to be a boy, even though everyone told me "you're a girl" based on my assigned sex. The thought stayed buried inside, never surfacing strongly, and I didn't feel much discomfort or anxiety about it.

The first sharp memory is elementary school, when I cut my hair short. I was especially happy that time; when people took me for a boy, I never explained myself. I just felt inside, "I guess it doesn't matter." In middle school, at puberty, everyone's secondary sex characteristics began to develop — the boys' voices changed, the girls' bodies changed — but I clearly grew anxious, especially because I was a bit early-blooming: breast development made me deeply resistant. I would buy chest binders online and flatten my chest, completely unlike other girls my age, who accepted their body changes.

For a while I thought I might be a "butch T" among lesbians — a masculine-dressing lesbian. But later I felt that wasn't right either: I had no particularly strong interest in women, and men seemed fine too. So was I bisexual? That question occupied my thoughts for a long time. By high school, I honestly wasn't that troubled by it, though occasionally I'd still be mistaken for a boy — but not often, since my voice is still fairly thin. Meanwhile, I also took part in feminist activities and threw myself into them.

What really made me see myself clearly came after I connected with some communities. I began to realize that, from childhood, my inner identification was actually male — purely male. Yet I also feel gender identity can be fluid. Over the years, with few negative external influences, I gradually accepted the parts of myself assigned female, but that doesn't mean I fully identify as a cisgender woman. So at this stage, my gender identity leans more toward "non-binary" and "agender" — all still in exploration.

As for my sexual orientation, my preferences seem to shift frequently; to this day I'm not sure which gender or type of person I prefer. Now, with the help of public-good organizations and communities, I've started HRT. But my goal isn't a complete "gender correction". One reason is that accessing medication in the current Chinese medical environment is genuinely difficult; another is that I'm not particularly distressed; and my position as non-binary means I won't consider full surgical transition for now — though I might consider chest-flattening surgery.

title: True and False
contentHtml: Back in the day, my political stance made me anti-trans; I couldn't even notice my own transgender inclinations. When my thinking finally opened up, I discovered that I was one of them all along. And so I accepted myself.

title: A Cat's First Birthday
contentHtml:
Reader note: this piece contains suicide content. Don't only ask why a person in despair chose the wrong escape; see what pushed them into a place with no right exit. If you're in a dark place right now, please don't force yourself to read this. Protecting your own heart is always what matters most.

Reader note: this piece contains overdose (OD) content. Only when safety, dignity, belonging, love, and physical and mental support truly exist can a person have a better choice than continuing to escape and suffer. If the text upsets you, please leave. You deserve to be treated equally and to heal gently.

Time really flies. Stopping to look back, I realized this shell of a body has carried me this far. Every footprint left along the way has now blossomed into flowers.

I still remember being in kindergarten, staring blankly at the other girls' little dresses. One day during nap time, a boy asked if I dared to wear a dress — and he really helped me borrow one from a girl. I put it on joyfully; the moment the skirt flared, I touched for the first time in this world a dream named "myself". After I woke from the dream, looking at the clothes in the wardrobe that belonged to a "boy", that longing I dared not speak of squeezed my chest till it ached. Until one summer day five years ago, I happened to click into the "crossdress masters forum". In that moment, it was like a ray of light piercing into the deep sea — I knew I wasn't a monster, and that there were others in this world searching for the light like me, meow…

In middle school, this body I dreaded grew breasts. That night, I wrapped myself in the blanket and felt the gentle rise of my chest with my palm. Even though me, the cat, understood nothing about medicine or transgender back then, and knew it might look "abnormal" to others — it was the very softest tenderness and miracle this shell that had always made me suffer had ever given me, in this cold world, yay.

Around then, I was lucky enough to hear about LGBT and learned that in this vast world there were so many people walking bravely ahead just to be themselves. In that hidden corner called Telegram, I quietly added the blue, pink and white colours to my nickname. Those three little colour blocks, though faint, were my silent declaration to myself.

Later, the "femboy" trend rose on Chinese internet. Watching those kindred souls showing their softness and cuteness on screen, my suppressed heart stirred again. Riding that wave, I finally gathered enough courage to quietly buy myself a simple pleated skirt.

Until last year, when I met a very gentle sister in all my confusion — the cat took that fateful step at last. I still remember that cloudy day, palms drenched in sweat. Carefully, from that pink box filled with the colour of hope, I pried out the first little yellow candy — Progynova — and swallowed it with warm water… And now, time slips by, and the cat applies clear estradiol gel to my skin every day with practiced ease, feeling the coolness melt into my blood; that cyproterone (CPA) I once found terrifying, the thing I couldn't even bear to look at, has become an ordinary daily object lying quietly on the corner of the desk, keeping the cat company 💊.

But, if only, I wish this were just a beautiful fairytale. Yet this long road really isn't a fairytale scattered with rose petals, meow… 💦

Going to the hospital for treatment, I was deeply stung by those appraising, stunned, even malicious gazes in the lobby; midway, I even ran into the most disgusting kind of creepy old man giving off the stench of sexual repression online… At that moment the cat was so scared, so close to retching, feeling as if I were being held down in a foul-smelling drain, and could only curl up in a corner…

In this circle full of hidden corners, I've also witnessed far too much blood and tears along other people's journeys. Watching on my social media feed the sisters who were thrown out of their homes after their families found out, or who mentally collapsed after running out of medication, the cat's heart is filled with deep sympathy — but more than that, a bone-chilling fear like the winter night wind😭. It's a Damoclean sword suspended overhead. Every night, the cat shrinks into a tiny ball, shivering under the covers, tears soaking through the pillow. Crying, I'd think: the cat's family conditions here are pretty ordinary by comparison — could the next one cruelly ground to dust by this ruthless world be silly me? I'm so, so tired; several times I almost couldn't hold on. The dark voice in my heart kept tempting: just give up… 💔

But! Thank goodness! The cat didn't die! [wiping the tears off my face] Finally, in the endless despair, I grabbed a lifeline — I met an incredibly gentle trans-friendly doctor! In that examination room reeking of disinfectant, we pinky-swore that I would legitimately get that white certificate of mine!

Then in early 2026, the cat forced out all of my self-discipline, gritted through the withdrawal symptoms, and quit the OD I'd been so deeply dependent on… Because the cat wants to greet the future with the clearest mind and the most beautiful, cleanest posture🥺

The process of asking the school to let me grow my hair long was like a war without gunpowder — countless arguments, tug-of-war, silent treatment, and breakdowns — but now, the cat won! I've got shoulder-length hair with a hint of rebelliousness, in a mullet! [the scent of shampoo lingers at my nose-tip]

The silly cat not only learned to use a straightener, carefully curling every strand against the mirror into beautiful waves, but also faithfully completed the tiresome skincare routine every single day. During New Year, clutching the New Year money I'd saved up, I gritted my teeth and spent over a thousand yuan on a whole pile of bottles and jars. Now the skincare products on my desk keep growing, giving off a faint floral scent… Looking at the self in the mirror with skin growing softer bit by bit, I really want to travel back in time and give that self, deep in appearance anxiety and afraid to even look in a mirror, a big hug🫂.

This year's cat has also been growing like crazy! In this little cyber world, my Twitter gained a full 1,000 followers! I'm now a small content creator with a 1K-follower account that people actually like🥰! I also went to the bank alone and got my first-ever Mastercard with my own name printed on it💳; I figured out complicated tutorials myself, set up a Japanese internet node🌐, and activated my sparkling Twitter Premium~

Not only that — the cat has been working to add gentle things to my little cat den. On the very last day before the IKEA in Ningbo relocated, the cat and a kindred soul rode for a long time to get there. Seeing the familiar blue-and-yellow signs everywhere, we picked for ages among the baskets and finally bought two soft, adorable shark plushies (Blåhaj). Even though all these sharks mercilessly "robbed" the cat's already thin wallet, when I held them tight in my arms and carried them all the way back to that cramped little room, my heart felt completely full. Now those two cute sharks lie obediently on the cat's bed. Even now, when strangers come and their unsparing gazes sweep over the cosmetics on my desk and the sharks on my bed, I no longer feel so scared or ashamed. Because at night, as long as I bury my face deep in the shark's belly, feeling that reassuring softness and slight suffocation, I can cling tightly to my dearest little E in my dreams.

The most, MOST surprising thing: the US stocks the cat was studying while staring at red-and-green candlestick charts at night actually returned a whopping 24%+! [rolling around happily on the bed] ps. The cat is under 18, so here I mean funds — after all, only when you get real silver and gold into your own hands can you truly break free of that suffocating cage called the birth family, and buy yourself freedom, plus that hot, fragrant McDonald's grilled chicken sandwich)

The cat has also silently set a must-win battle: in the future, I must save enough money to get orthognathic surgery, and I MUST do SRS! I will save money desperately in the days ahead, and finish this formidable mission before little E heads to university. These are the mountains the cat must cross in order to take back this body that always belonged to me, and to prove myself to the world.

Standing at this very moment, I can finally try to erase those rigid gender concepts from my mind, letting the gender dysphoria that tormented me through countless nights dissipate like morning mist. Although my body still trudges heavily toward so-called MTF with the help of medication, the cat slowly feels… those labels stuck on me from outside don't matter anymore, meow. I don't need to be defined by the rigid words "boy" or "girl".

I'm just a cat. A cat who loves little E, who wants to wiggle through the other end of the net and keep them company even across the screen. I'm just a cat who wants to be gently petted on the head, who wants to live desperately and work hard for herself🐈.

Looking back at this whole year: stumbling, knees all muddy, hands covered with tears, fear, and scratches from broken glass — but I made it through, meow! Thank you for staying with me in this world, and little E, who makes me feel safe even doing nothing at all. And thank you to the self who gritted through countless deep nights crying, and never once gave up.

Now the shell is 17.

And the cat is 1…

title: Escaping Shang Jingwei
contentHtml:
I am writing this to condemn the inhumane treatment I received at the Shanghai Mental Health Center, and to warn those who come after. The shadow of Shang Jingwei has never faded from me — not one bit.

This article is written entirely from my real experiences and carries the nature of a memoir. No matter how absurd a detail may seem, it truly happened. To protect the privacy of those involved, some information has been blurred; details involving self-harm, suicide, and dangerous objects are likewise rendered non-operational.

I. Police at the Bedside

When I woke up, there were two police officers standing by my bed.

My consciousness was still floating in a thin fog. The dizziness from the previous night's medication hadn't fully cleared; the ceiling, the wardrobe, and the two unfamiliar faces all seemed to sit behind frosted glass. I stared at them for a few seconds before I understood what those uniforms meant.

Police officers appearing in a bedroom usually don't bring good news.

"Awake?" One of them called my name. "Do you know why we're here?"

"No."

"Were you posting extreme statements online again yesterday?"

I didn't answer.

In that instant, I already guessed what had happened. The suicide letter I'd sent the day before had likely been seen by someone, who passed it on to my parents or the police. During that period I had been constantly searching for highly toxic chemicals. I had severe depression, anxiety, and suicidal tendencies. Now, those thoughts hidden in search histories, chat windows, and delivery pages had finally crossed the screen and become the two people standing beside my bed.

"No," I said.

My parents stood in the doorway with the look I knew well but never wanted to face: worry, exhaustion, and a fear of not knowing what to do with me.

"Get dressed. Come with us for a ride."

"Where to?"

"The Shanghai Mental Health Center."

"Can I not go?"

"No."

There was no room to argue. I dressed and went downstairs. Two officers flanked me left and right, another walking ahead. It looked less like an escort than an escort under arrest. In the underground garage, I sat in the back seat of the police car while my parents followed in their own.

This was probably my third or fourth ride in a police car. The earlier ones also had to do with suicide. My memory of the times has blurred, leaving only similar car doors, similar silence, and the streets receding outside the window.

There were three officers in the car. The body-worn camera pointed at me. I held my phone but dared not light the screen. I had taken the road to "Jingwei" more than once, but in the past it had been the family car, a taxi, or an ambulance. Only this time, through the police car's window, I watched the familiar elevated highway, intersections, and plane trees slide past one by one.

Shanghai ran on as usual. Only my life was being carried toward a door that would lock shut behind me.

II. Signing

The police car stopped in front of the outpatient building. The officers brought me into the emergency department, cut through the crowd, pushed to the very front of the line, and quickly conferred with the staff. I stood aside while the other two officers watched me, like guarding an object that might go out of control at any moment.

Jingwei's emergency room wasn't unfamiliar to me. Before, I had seen emotionally agitated people being brought in, shouting and screaming. I would instinctively avert my gaze back then, thinking they belonged to a world different from mine. Now I stood in the same place and suddenly realized that, in other people's eyes, I had become one of those people who need to be avoided.

The lead officer went to the "serious illness registration" window first, then after a moment walked toward "admission registration." At the sight of those words, my heart sank.

"I'm not staying in the hospital." I raised my voice. "Being admitted will only make me worse."

Nobody stopped what they were doing.

The papers were handed over one by one, the forms filled in one by one, until only the guardian's signature remained. My mother had cried herself unable to speak; her hand shook too much to hold the pen.

"Don't listen to him. Sign it," the officer said.

"No!"

The officer looked at me. "This is for your own good. We believe in science; the hospital will cure you."

"How can you be so sure?"

"Because we believe in science."

"You'll thank us when you're discharged," said one of the police.

Those words were like a needle, piercing precisely the last shred of my sanity. I glared at my parents and spoke the words most able to hurt them and most clearly my defiance, making my final struggle: "If you commit me, I will find every way to die. As soon as I'm discharged, I'll kill myself."

Both parents were crying.

The officers urged my mother to sign. Her hand trembled the whole time; my father took the pen, then, at a loss, handed it back to her. At last, my mother, as if suddenly draining her last strength, wiped away her tears.

"I'll sign. I'll sign!"

The instant the pen tip touched the paper, I knew there was no turning back.

Begging was useless, and escape was impossible. Three officers guarded the sides; I couldn't even find a single direction to break through. Desperation had nowhere to go and finally turned back onto my own body. I clawed at my wrist with my fingernails over and over until the skin broke.

"What are you doing!"

An officer noticed and grabbed my hand immediately; the others closed in. They forced my arms apart, controlled me left and right, and took me toward the inpatient building.

Along the way, people turned to look. Some gazes held curiosity, some alarm. For a moment I felt a strange thrill, as if as long as others feared me, I still possessed some power. But the feeling vanished quickly. This admission pressed down on me like a boulder, leaving no room to think of anything else.

At the inpatient building's entrance there was a checkpoint, with "No Forcing Through" painted on the wall and several security guards nearby. The elevator took us up to the twelfth floor. The elevator hall held only a steel door leading to the ward, locked; an officer rang the bell. After a while, a nurse came out and took the thick stack of papers.

"New patient?"

"Yes, all the procedures are here."

The steel door opened. I was brought inside, and the door closed behind me.

The sound wasn't loud, but it was like a stamp falling onto a long stretch of my life to come.

III. Ward Twelve

Between the elevator hall and the ward there was still a buffer zone — glass partitions, security doors, access controls, one layer wrapped inside the next. It reminded me of a laboratory observation area: the people outside can see in, but those inside can never touch the outside world.

The admission check began with a body search. I was ordered to remove all my clothes; medical staff examined my body and took photographs for the records. My own clothes and shoes were taken away and replaced with an oversized hospital gown and plastic slippers. Nothing could be kept; nothing truly belonged to me; only this body of mine was left.

The ward was more dilapidated than I had imagined. The wall plaster was peeling off in large chunks, exposing cold grey concrete; the walls bore dark stains from dampness, muddy in colour, like some stain that could never be washed clean. Another wall was covered with scrawled writing — some still barely readable, some with no connection to one another, as if many people had left their broken thoughts there.

My bed was near the door, far from the window. The little sunlight and cityscape outside couldn't reach me. Iron bars were on the window, and no extra objects were to be found in the room. The air held a stale, damp smell, mixed with disinfectant and the breath of a place long unventilated.

I only learned later that I had been assigned Level 1 nursing care — the highest level here.

After changing clothes, I was led into the corridor. On both sides stood rows of restraint chairs: wooden, heavy, with armrests, and a chest board that could fold down and lock. Once you sat in one and the board came down, it was very hard to stand again. Fellow patients sat quietly in their own places — mostly middle-aged and older; the young were few, and minors like me even rarer. Their gaze was uniformly sluggish; they only lifted their heads to glance at me as I passed, then looked away.

I too was locked into one of those chairs. The armrest behind me was broken, hollow inside, filled with dust, and there were cockroaches crawling about. One of them crawled onto my chair; I could only lean as far forward as I could and pray it wouldn't climb onto me.

"Restrain him."

Two cloth straps bound my wrists, fixing my hands to the armrests.

That was around three in the afternoon. Until six in the evening, I sat there. No phone, no book, no conversation, nothing to occupy my attention. I could only look at the wall, at the lamplight falling on the floor tiles, at nurses and patients in yellow vests passing back and forth.

Time for the first time showed its true, terrifying shape. It wasn't the numbers on a clock, but a blankness without boundaries. Inside it, a person can neither advance nor retreat; they can only stay awake, waiting for the next minute to repeat the last.

When dinner came, I didn't eat a bite, and I refused the water too. The food looked even worse than school meals. Refusing food was one of the very few ways to control that I could still find.

The nurse warned me: "If you don't eat, we'll have to take medical measures."

"I don't care."

She asked me at least to drink water. I kept refusing, and in the end water was forced into my mouth. I coughed a few times; swallowing was like a failed resistance.

That evening came the blood draws. Because I was newly admitted, there were many tests — one tube after another. The needle hurt, but I was too weary to react. I noticed that some of the people pushing the meal carts, moving supplies, and tidying things were not medical staff at all, but fellow patients in yellow vests. They seemed to know this order better than I did, and understood when to lower their heads and when to stay silent.

At nine the lights went out. The restraints on my wrists had just been removed when I was taken back to the bed, my four limbs strapped separately to the bed frame. My body lay forced open, unable to turn over. The discomfort of medication withdrawal and the stress of a new admission piled on top of each other — and above my head hung a fluorescent light that never went out through the night.

I stared at the wall with open eyes, unable to fall asleep.

I thought of my life before, of what crime I had committed, why I had ended up here. Grievance, rage, and fear churned through my body over and over, until all that was left was a very faint crying. I didn't dare cry too loud; it felt as though even sorrow would be registered and evaluated, then answered with harsher handling.

Around three in the morning I finally lost consciousness. At five, the nursing assistant woke me.

IV. Fixed Time

In the early morning, still not awake, I was roused loudly by the nurse, my mind blank. The assistant undid the bed restraints, but the straps stayed on my wrists. I dragged them along to brush my teeth and wash my face; every motion became clumsy. When that was done, I was taken back to the corridor, into that chair, and strapped in again. I propped my heavy, sleepy head up with one hand and leaned forward as far as I could to keep from touching the cockroaches on the back of the chair.

Breakfast came at six. I still refused to eat. When the assistant took away the untouched bowl of porridge, he glanced at me. I couldn't tell whether it was anger or disgust.

That morning I was taken for a chest X-ray. When we left the ward, my hands were bound together and led by a strap. The special elevator descended; the doors opened and different light and voices appeared at the end of the corridor. Looking back later, that short trip to radiology counted as the most "interesting" experience I had in Ward Twelve. How bored must a person be to treat a chest X-ray as a break?

Back to the ward, and sitting again. No lunch, no dinner. The medical staff began giving me fluids. The clear liquid dripped down slowly along the line; I watched it enter my veins, without resistance and without gratitude. The second night, I stared at the wall again. On the third day, because I had kept not eating, I received more examinations and fluids. The overnight infusion somehow caused my blood sugar to spike abnormally the next day.

I no longer knew whom I was punishing. At first I thought the hunger strike was a fight against the hospital, my parents, and the form I had signed; only later did I understand that the first to be drained was always me. Yet I also felt I deserved it — so stupid, to have let a mental illness and suicidal tendencies be seen by others. I, of all people, was best at hiding emotions.

It was garbage-collection time. The assistant piled all kinds of waste in the corridor and dragged out a stinking bedsheet — the work of the seventy- or eighty-year-old patient next door, who had lost all ability to care for himself and had defecated on the sheet. For half an hour of cleaning, even for the hour after, the whole corridor reeked of faeces and decay.

That afternoon, a new patient came to Ward Ten. He was angrier than anyone here, insisting he was perfectly fine — that he'd merely lost his temper with his family once and was sent here. Actually, based on how he described what happened, I even felt his anger was entirely reasonable. He kept trying to break free, shouting and making a scene. Nobody paid him any attention.

That night, the new patient roared all night, shaking his bed, demanding to call the police. I couldn't fall asleep at all.

The third afternoon, my parents came to visit. The moment they walked into the ward, my hands still bound, sitting on the bed, I burst into tears.

That was probably the most disheveled I had cried in my sixteen years. I couldn't explain why I was crying. I wept until I couldn't breathe, saying over and over that I couldn't take it; tears and snot soaked the bedsheet. My parents, seeing me like that, promised to try to move me to a better ward.

I got my phone back briefly and immediately messaged a few people I was close to: "I've been committed against my will. I'm going crazy." There followed many more words about death. I wasn't asking for help then — at least not subjectively; I more wanted to end myself to escape the torment. But looking back now, every message I sent out was, in some sense, waiting for someone to catch me.

After the visit ended, I was taken to a meeting room about twenty medical students sat inside, each with pen and paper. At the head of the long table sat a chief physician and an assisting physician. I was placed beside them, restraint straps still on my wrists.

The assisting physician read out my medical history aloud: depression, gender-identity-related distress, drug abuse, and several suicide risk events. The things that had only been said in whispers in a consulting room were read out item by item, turned into material for everyone to record.

The chief physician began to question me. From my upbringing to what had happened recently; from why I depended on medication to why I wanted to become a girl; from when that wish began to why I wanted to die. One question after another, taking me apart piece by piece into symptoms, triggers, a timeline, and diagnostic grounds.

To some questions I told the truth; to others I lied. I kept my expression as calm as possible. I had once been good at debating and knew how to organize language under pressure, and how to give answers that sounded reasonable. That little ability became my last armor in that moment.

The chief physician delivered the analysis; the students bent their heads to write. I, however, understood clearly: in this moment I was not only a patient but a case — a lesson plan unfolding live. Truly worthy of the country's best psychiatric hospital.

That night, I had the first glimmer of hope. My parents said I might be moved to Ward Fourteen the next day.

Around ten at night, I still couldn't sleep, sitting on the bed looking at the mottled wall. My entire time in Ward Twelve, no doctor had come to understand my condition, no one had prescribed antidepressants or sleeping pills; they'd simply locked me in here. There was no treatment effect at all — instead it left me with deep psychological trauma. Is this what the so-called "most advanced" psychiatric care looks like?

V. Ward Fourteen

The next day I woke at five as usual and forced down a few spoonfuls of porridge. At noon, finding my mood somewhat stabilized, the doctors completed the handover between Ward Twelve and Ward Fourteen, and I was taken upstairs.

Ward Fourteen was called the "VIP ward." The moment I walked in, I felt an almost absurd contrast: intact walls, soft lighting, less murky air — it finally felt like an ordinary hospital. The restraints were removed, I changed back into my own clothes, I could shower every day, use my phone, and even have family order meals for me.

If I'd never been to Ward Twelve, these might have been the most ordinary details of life; coming out of there, they felt like luxuries.

I used my phone vindictively, like taking back every minute I'd lost. My parents ordered me a wagyu rice bowl. The first mouthful went down, and I realized I hadn't truly eaten in a long time. My stomach protested, but my sense of taste felt reborn. That meal ended my near-week-long hunger strike.

My new attending doctor was surnamed Chen. She would remain my doctor afterwards. She asked many questions, yet her tone stayed gentle throughout, never treating each statement as a danger signal needing immediate subduing. She reworked the treatment plan, prescribing sedation, anti-anxiety, and sleep-improving medication.

At that moment I thought: this is what I imagined "Jingwei" should have been.

The next day, a tablet was brought in. I could listen to music, scroll, and watch anime — superficially reconnected to my old life. But what Ward Twelve left in me didn't vanish because the environment got better. When a lock clicked, when a nurse's footsteps quickened, when someone came close to the bed, I tensed up instantly. My body remembered, ahead of my mind, the feel of being pinned down, bound, and of staring at a wall all night.

I began chatting frequently with someone online. She was about my age, also struggling with gender identity and depression, and a champion in chemistry competitions. She was out of town then, and I kept asking her for sodium azide. I described death like a concrete plan, as if a sufficiently rigorous plan would let me reclaim control of my fate.

A few days later she returned to Shanghai and came to see me in the hospital at once. That was our first offline meeting. She gave me much comfort, and also brought the thing I had asked her for. To this day I am still deeply grateful to her.

Before leaving the ward, she secretly told the nurse about my suicidal intent.

The staff acted immediately. I was strapped to the bed again, and my phone was taken. In that instant, the memories of Ward Twelve flooded back. I was terrified, furious, and felt betrayed. The doctors searched the room thoroughly, but never found the small paper-wrapped pouch of sodium nitrite hidden in my trouser pocket.

That night, during a gap between rounds, I swallowed it.

Sodium nitrite goes down cold and smooth, slightly salty, with a hint of sweetness. My heart rate climbed, my head felt light, then turned to a headache. My heart pounded harder; I felt palpitations and anxiety, my breathing quickened, my consciousness blurred, my body lost its strength, and slight convulsions began. The nurses noticed something was wrong, and the ward instantly became noisy. Someone called a doctor, someone readied oxygen, someone phoned for an ambulance. I could hear the sounds, but my brain had lost the capacity to understand them.

And then the lights, the corridor, and the faces all broke off.

VI. After Midnight

Around midnight on May 11, I was admitted to the intensive care unit at Zhongshan Hospital.

Consciousness briefly floated up, as if a last flash before the end. I felt many instruments and tubes being quickly attached to my body. I heard doctors and nurses talking at the rescue bed: my skin was turning purple, my limbs convulsing, my vital signs very poor, methemoglobin exceeding the instrument's upper limit — 70 percent.

I couldn't respond. Couldn't speak, couldn't move my fingers, couldn't even blink. Breathing no longer fully belonged to me.

Someone said my convulsions needed sedatives. Then the voices drifted away again.

A coma is not sleep. Sleep may still have dreams, a murky sense of time; a coma has nothing. Not even darkness, because darkness is still a sensation. There was only a void impossible to describe. By the time I had consciousness again, two days had passed.

Around three in the morning on May 13, I woke up.

The moment I woke, I couldn't control my own body. A tube was in my windpipe; catheters ran through my nose and body. Every breath brought a foreign sensation; the vapor of my breath condensed and flowed back along the tube wall, like drowning and choking. When a nurse cleared my secretions, a thin tube went deep into my throat; the discomfort nearly broke me again.

After seven in the morning, a doctor judged my vital signs essentially stable and gradually removed the tracheal tube and other catheters. My hands were still strapped to the bed, mainly to prevent accidents before my consciousness fully returned.

After surviving, what came first was not epiphany but boredom.

My parents and teachers came to visit; seeing me awake, they all visibly relaxed. When the visit ended, I could only lie in bed. With nothing to do, I borrowed a book from a nurse — "ICU Ultrasound Manual," the only book here — and read it. A doctor asked which middle school I attended and how my grades were. I mentioned my middle-school exam scores and my experience in physics and informatics competitions. They praised me as clever, saying I looked like a genius.

That was the first time since entering high school that I had heard such words again. Lying on the ICU bed, just back from death's edge, I felt a faint excitement at a long-missed affirmation. Now that I think of it, the excitement was both absurd and real. A sixteen-year-old's self-esteem can always revive in the most inappropriate places.

On the 14th, my parents sent me an e-reader and a paperback novel, "Super Kaguya-hime." I killed time reading, often until late at night. The characters in the story crossed worlds and were reborn, while I lay in the sound of the monitors, turning pages one by one, temporarily not thinking about why I was still alive.

On the morning of the 15th, the doctor announced I was out of danger and could leave the ICU.

The ambulance took me back to the Shanghai Mental Health Center.

VII. Leaving

Because I had just attempted suicide, after returning to Ward Fourteen I was again under strict restraint. My hands and feet were strapped to the bed; my range of movement was only a little space around the mattress.

I can no longer recall precisely how long that period lasted. My memory was sliced into similar fragments by medication, sleep, and a repeat routine. Every day: reading, scrolling videos, receiving ward rounds, occasionally talking to my parents. Compared to Ward Twelve, conditions were far better — but "far better" does not equal bearable.

My mood deteriorated bit by bit. Losing control of my own body for so long made me more and more agitated. The more the staff feared I would hurt myself, the more they needed to restrain me; the stricter the restraint, the more I felt I was no longer a person but a risk; the angrier and more defiant I became, the more convinced they were that the restraint was necessary. We were trapped in a loop that kept proving itself to each other.

Finally, one day I woke up and could bear it no longer. I fought loudly with my parents, insisting on leaving. I began undoing the straps myself. A nurse noticed, called the assistants, tied me up again, pushed my bed out to the nurse's station in the corridor, and put protective gloves on me.

I kept struggling, even managing to pull the gloves off. Assistants came to control me; I fought desperately. Someone warned that if I continued, they'd use sedatives. The argument grew fiercer, and finally the head nurse stepped in and called my parents aside.

I saw my parents crying again.

The first time, at the admission signing, they wept as they sent me in; this time, they wept as they agreed to let me out. Between those two sets of tears lay the steel door of Ward Twelve, the window of Ward Fourteen, the ICU, and one death almost fully carried out.

The next day, the procedures were done. I changed into my own clothes, got my belongings back, and followed my parents through the ward's access gates into the elevator. The numbers fell floor by floor. Walking out of the inpatient building, I learned what it felt like to be released from prison.

At last I had left Jingwei.

But leaving was not like an escape in the movies. No running, no pursuit, no victory music. I just walked beside my parents, slowly, toward the parking spot. The city was as noisy as ever; vehicles still passed through the intersection; everything was the same as on the day I was brought here.

For a long time, I understood the whole experience as pure imprisonment. I remember the name I was forced to sign, the iron doors and restraint straps, the light burning all night, and how my privacy became a case file in front of a room full of strangers. Nor can I deny that someone later noticed my abnormality in the ward, someone gave me oxygen in the ambulance, someone pulled me back from the brink in the ICU.

My parents said I'd thank them after discharge. I didn't suddenly thank everything as they'd hoped, nor did surviving automatically make me love life. The thought of death didn't vanish on discharge day, and the fear the wards left behind didn't end with the closing of the steel door. Real recovery takes much longer than one rescue; it is far more complex than the four characters "believe in science."

What "escaping" came to mean for me later has another layer. It wasn't merely leaving a building, nor beating the doctors, nurses, police, or parents. It was slowly stepping back from that dead end where the only way to prove you still had choices was to hurt yourself; it was admitting that the sixteen-year-old me was both furious and afraid, both wanting to die and, time after time, still sending messages to others; it was allowing the person who had been strapped to a bed not to remain forever on that bed.

To this day, when falling asleep, I still feel the near-death sensation of swallowing salt. I still dream of Ward Twelve's corridor. In the dream, the steel door locks behind me, the light is pale white, and time stands still. I look for an exit again and again, and each time I wake to find that outside the window, it is already dawn.

I write this not to prove how close I came to death, nor to dress my suffering in a medal worth showing off. I only want to give that chaotic memory a shape, and to give myself — the one who was never genuinely heard back then — one full chance to speak.

I did leave Jingwei in the end.

But my soul died inside it.

title: A Boy Currently Carving Himself
contentHtml:
Reader note: this piece contains suicide content. Don't only ask why a person in despair chose the wrong escape; see what pushed them into a place with no right exit. If you're in a dark place right now, please don't force yourself to read this. Protecting your own heart is always what matters most.

I am [nickname hidden]. At age 11, I was violated. After family bankruptcy, I was beaten until I sat on the windowsill, wanting to jump. After that, the [nickname hidden] in my body handed the reins to me — a boy. She was the original; I came later. Neither of us disappeared; we just share one body. In grades 7 and 8, my Chinese teacher said my writing was good and encouraged me to write argumentative essays. In grade 9 the teacher changed; then there was only dictation and formulaic material. I like math because it never changes face, unlike life. My mom knows my identity and has talked about taking me to get puberty blockers — but she's dragged it out for half a year. I couldn't take it; since early February this year I've been using hormones on my own. My periods stopped, and my body has finally started moving in the "right" direction. But we fought, we raged, we called the police, we signed agreements. She says she loves me, but her love knows how to stab. I have friends. They joined me on a half-hour hunt for an accessible toilet, and they didn't run away when I lost my mind. They make me feel this broken Earth Online isn't worth deleting my account over yet. I have a little over a month until the high-school entrance exam. I don't know if I'll get into a key school, whether I can wear boys' uniforms in high school, or whether my mom will really take me to the hospital. But I know one thing: I'm not a monster. I'm a boy still carving himself — unfinished, but refusing to stop. Thank you for reading this far.

Even educational content is a way of promoting the circle — once they're curious, they'll go look it up, and then it's beyond control. That day at lunch I was so furious I cried.

title: Living Under a Different Identity
contentHtml: Once, this was the hardest period of my life — four major blows in a row, to the point I basically lost my hold on living. I hurt myself in many ways; sometimes nothing happened, only the pain proving this was real. There was even a time I saw the tunnel with the light at the end, yet I still didn't die. Although things have stabilized a lot now… sometimes I still fall into anxiety. I hope I can slowly get better — since I've already made my decision: to live under a different identity.

title: The Mirror Image I Brushed Past
contentHtml: In middle school I met someone named Deng**, just like me in every way. But because I transferred schools, we went our separate ways and never met again.

title: The Blooming Season That Will Come
contentHtml: We all have a blooming season — earlier or later; as long as we nurture it, it will eventually open. It has been ten years since I came out to my parents. I once suffered depression, dropped out of school, and stood at the edge of ending myself several times. Until two years ago, when I truly faced my gender dysphoria and embraced myself — I finally made it to renewal and blossoming. With serenity, accept what cannot be changed; with courage, change what can be changed; with wisdom, tell the two apart.

title: Gentle Resonance Across the Dinner Table
contentHtml: Last time I went out to eat with my family — because I have long hair, a fairly androgynous look, and the new toiletries I'd been using — maybe blood runs thicker than water, and my mom asked me: "I feel your life habits moving more and more toward the feminine. Do you want to be a girl?" My feelings at that moment were tangled; I didn't know what my family thought, but how we treat each other matters so much to me, so I answered: "How could that be! I just think this look suits me." Then she replied: "Haha! I see — looks like I was overthinking. But, you're my flesh and blood; even if you wanted to transition, I would support you." I was deeply moved on the spot, but I felt conflicted: "Should I tell them? Or was it just a joke?" I'm still wondering even now — if I truly confessed, how would they see me?

title: Walking Out of the Maze Like a Dam Bursting
contentHtml: About the question asking at what age I confirmed my gender identity: since childhood I had the idea of wanting to be a girl, but I always talked myself out of it. As a kid I read Dream of the Red Chamber, and when I saw that even Jia Baoyu said, "When I see girls, I feel refreshed; when I see men, I find them stinking and oppressive," I figured: well then, every boy must hate being a boy too! So I just muddled along, letting myself be. I dawdled until I was 18; one day, out of nowhere, I told my then-girlfriend I wanted to get sex-change surgery. She said people who do transition surgery die in their thirties. So I talked myself out of it again — I was even cowardly enough not to look it up online. Later I learned what LGBT is, and even argued online with people who were homophobic and transphobic, yet I was still silly enough to never look inside my own heart. It wasn't until I later went abroad that I accidentally wandered into RLE.wiki one day — and the dysphoria hit me like a dam bursting, washing me senseless. By then I was already 23.
