title: The Memoir of Hosino Neko
contentHtml:
This article is republished from the author's personal blog hosinoneko.me, under the CC BY 4.0 Creative Commons license.

WARNING! This article is not yet finished. The author plans to complete the part covering up to high school in September–October of Minguo 114 (2025), and to finish the whole thing in April of Minguo 115 (2026).

Preface

Who am I?

Although my homepage already introduces me, as a standalone article I'll introduce myself again.

My name is Hosino Neko (星野寧子) — maybe a girl, and I like being treated as a little cat. I love playing Minecraft. Previously, for "witnessing" something, I was invited by the Chinese police for a full pot of tea; after finishing the tea I still didn't repent, went witnessing again and was caught a second time; afterwards I became MtF. (As of September 9, Minguo 114 / 2025)

Why am I writing this?

I don't know. Maybe so that if I disappear, someone can understand the whole arc of who I am. Or: even if I die, I want to leave something of mine in the world (hoping GitHub and Vercel won't go bankrupt the instant I die or something).

Maybe I was also influenced by Se-meimei's memoir; if so, let me just quote directly:

I don't know why I'm writing this — maybe I want to dump these messy memories out in advance, so that after a suicide no one will ever know of them.

Who Se-meimei is — I'll say later.

If I disappear, what I want to leave behind

  1. 心做し (Kokoronashi)

Timeline

Born: Minguo 97 (2008), August 8

Primary school: Minguo 103 (2014) September – Minguo 109 (2020) summer — graduated

Middle school: Minguo 109 September – Minguo 112 (2023) summer — graduated

High school: Minguo 112 September – Minguo 114 (2025) summer — nominally graduated

First RLE attempt: Minguo 114 September 14, at night

First HRT: Minguo 114 September 24

Sent to a correction institution: Minguo 114 October 3 – Minguo 115 (2026) February 11

Escape to Shanghai: Minguo 115 February 14 – Minguo 115 May 9

Schools

Somewhere Normal University Affiliated Primary School — Minguo 103 September – Minguo 107 summer

HS — Minguo 107 September – Minguo 113 summer; graduated Minguo 115 June.

An international school in Qingdao — Minguo 113 September – early July Minguo 114

Gender dysphoria start: Minguo 114 July

The "Main Text"?

Early Childhood

Spawn

According to legend, I came into this world in a room inside my second uncle's company. I don't know if he has moved away by now; in any case, I've roughly completely forgotten where the room was.

I was born in a small county town in Shandong. The pace of life was neither fast nor slow, just right: no small-village acquaintance society, no big-city life pressure. Everything seemed just right.

My family first lived in the innermost building of our own company. Every day I played in the little garden of my father's company. The employees loved playing with me.

Sadly, a new office building was later built over that little garden (it's actually had quite a few years on it now), and the house we first lived in has likely been converted into a warehouse or something. Many of the people I once knew have left or retired. Some old employees are still there — but many of them I've forgotten who's who. Yet they remember me.

Third-Aunt Grandma

Everyone has their own "morning flowers, evening harvest", right?

After that, for a period I was sent to live with Third-Aunt Grandma in the countryside.

That was probably the happiest time of my life.

Although I could already remember things then, now it's all very vague. I've been back a few times in recent years, and Third-Aunt Grandma told me bits and pieces of that time. One thing she told me that stuck deeply: one night I was crying and making noise; the adults sneaked a corn from someone else's field, and when I got home I pestered to eat it, so they steamed it for me to gnaw on. At that time I loved playing with a certain older girl; once she had me try roller-skating, and even then I could only glide a little while holding her hand.

Funny thing: I naively thought I had only one sister, and after leaving, I envied everyone else for having a real older sister to play with every day. My understanding then: having a sister was the happiest thing in the world. Until I later learned that my first-uncle's house had a female cousin.

Back then I also learned to drive an electric tricycle (yes — the kind you see all over third-tier cities and villages); it was one of my proudest achievements. Once we went to the fields to irrigate, and on the way back a few farmers passed on their tricycle and greeted us with:

"Hey! Is a little kid allowed to drive the car?" (Shandong accent) Third-Aunt Grandma: "Sure, sure, he's real good at it" (Shandong accent)

When my mother came to take me back to the city, I even drove her to the market.

Who is Third-Aunt Grandma? Even now I've never sorted out what relation she is to me, and I've even forgotten her name. Growing up, I've never had a right opportunity — or rather, never knew how to bring it up.

Primary School

My family should count as petty bourgeois: my father is a merchant, and my mother is quite a virtuous wife. Income was considerable. For peers of the same class, schooling could be handled casually, muddle through for the degree, take over dad's business, buy an apartment, marry someone — and their whole life would be stable.

But it happened that my father and I both didn't want me to live this life out so blandly.

If you don't take a bite, you'll never know if it tastes like a piece of shit.

Remember these words, because they drove most of my decisions later.

Normal University Affiliated Primary School

I clearly remember that morning: my father woke me early; after breakfast, I thought we'd go to kindergarten as usual. But the car didn't turn left like usual as we went out the gate — it turned right, against the norm. Were we going to see Grandpa? Soon the car stopped, not having gone far.

I was taken to a strange place: primary school. Walking through the gate, my heart pounded — pure fear of the new environment. I was taken to a room (classroom), surrounded entirely by kids about my size, and then Dad left.

I don't know how long I was afraid, or what I was like when I got home; in any case, I began a childhood which, at the time, I thought was not very good.

I first attended the preschool class, and I was even the class monitor. Nothing much to brag about.

One impression stayed very strong: I secretly brought a little toy to school (I've forgotten what it was — probably one of those toys from a Kinder Surprise egg). The teacher found it, threw it out the window. There were iron bars on our classroom window, so even though we were on the first floor, I could only watch my toy lying out there with other scattered toys. I kept it on my mind for half a semester.

Another time, I sharpened a very sharp pencil and waved it around the class like a sword. Carelessly, the lead jabbed right into my arm. To this day you can still faintly see that scar.

Another time, the whole family went out for teppanyaki. I picked up my cup — unaware it was my cousin's beer glass. I took a big gulp and nearly threw up; I never imagined beer tasted like this.

That day had more beyond that: after dinner, the cousins were play-fighting outside the door. I poked my head out a little and was knocked flat by a cousin dashing toward me, my head banged against the door lock, leaving a scar.

Actually, I don't dislike this scar. In a certain sense, maybe it's a unique marker of mine (？)

This was the most beautiful time of my entire primary school. Because, in the following six years, I held the position of last in class.

My parents later said that because I hadn't attended a bridging class, I was sent to school a year early, so I didn't have advantages in various aspects. Of course this conflicts with what I said just now. I don't know which is right.

At that time this school had an extremely high reputation among locals. The school had two principals; one was my father's classmate (though I never mentioned it, I think I got in through his connection to my father). That vice-principal also taught us politics (called "Morality and Life" back then).

The other principal looked past fifty — a classic Mediterranean hairline, clearly a man not to be messed with.

Around fourth grade, once I was play-fighting with someone. The corridor was full of kids, noisy — but he spotted us at a glance. I noticed the principal first and frantically alerted the other guy; he didn't see, and the principal was already walking toward us. At the last moment he saw the principal and dashed back into the classroom with a "whoosh".

The principal surely saw, so he called the kid out at the classroom door. I tried poking my head out to a peek — and got a hard kick from that person. I completely couldn't understand what that was for. Then, as usual: lecture us first, then have the class monitor take us to the homeroom teacher, who lectured us again. What the monitor told the teacher — I remember it exactly:

"The two of them were running around in the corridor and got caught by the principal." "What the hell, we were play-wrestling, not running." In the end the punishment was copying classical poems.

I will never forget that kick and that line: "The two of them were running around in the corridor and got caught by the principal."

In short, because of my grades and my so-called naughtiness, I became a "bad kid" in the teachers' minds.

Homework lasted past midnight every day; too many errors in dictation meant a butt-spanking; during the day I was a thorn in the teachers' eyes. During those Normal University-Affiliate years, even in a third-grade class of over 40 kids, I made only two friends — and I hadn't even learned everyone's names by the end of the semester. One I met in grade 1; his father worked at my father's company, so we're still in touch — my childhood buddy. The other, met in grade 3; no contact since. Though I wasn't quite a lone wolf, the group games children play — like house — I basically never joined.

Moving House

We moved twice. The first time, from the company to a housing estate: a three-bedroom, one-living-room flat (3LDK in Japanese terms). That was probably before kindergarten.

Likely because of my younger brother's and sister's births, the three-bedroom got crowded. Around fourth grade, my father bought a personal iron bed and had me sleep in the living room. Since that wasn't a long-term plan, my father also bought a detached four-story villa on the east side of the city, and the whole family except me moved there. I didn't move immediately because of school; instead, they brought my grandfather over to keep me company. Later my grandfather returned to his old place, and I moved into the new house — for the last stretch of fourth grade, I took a taxi to school every day.

Transferring Schools

That summer of fourth grade, my father sat with me in the yard discussing transferring. He said he'd found three more schools, all outside the city, and asked if I'd go. I hesitated for a while, then agreed.

All three schools had entrance exams; the second one also had an interview.

On the first sitting, I failed all three.

Afterwards, I tried again for the second school (HS).

In my second sitting, a teacher walked over to interview me. He sat across from me, picked up the ruler set I'd brought, took out the straight ruler and the 60° set-square, stood the ruler upright, placed the triangle atop it — forming an arrow shape pointing north — and asked me: "What does this look like?" I looked, and instinctively said: "Like a tree." He smiled, then turned the whole shape sideways into an arrow pointing right, and asked again what it looked like. He might have been nudging me toward saying "an arrow", but I didn't catch on, thought for a moment and said: "Like a fallen tree." Only after he repeated the question did I realize it was an arrow.

This teacher was very special; a large part of his influence still shapes who I am now.

But anyway, I passed, and from September started fifth grade. Later I heard it was my father's banquet table and money-power doing the work.

HS

The Remaining Two Years of Childhood

The new school was in Weifang's high-tech zone — a true arrival "in the city", for me. The school was boarding. Yes: I started boarding in fifth grade.

What made me happy: I was finally no longer last in class. But not much higher — I was second from last. And in group assignments, I often got paired with the last-place kid.

I still hadn't changed: if someone noticed me, I'd play with them; if not, I stayed alone...

Brother Quan

Why call him "Brother Quan"? It was the school's habit, or tradition: calling teachers "Brother Quan" or "Sister Ying" and the like — quite a gangster feel. Nobody calls them that anymore now.

Brother Quan was our grade director — also the math teacher of the next class plus its "chief mentor". (In this school, homeroom teachers aren't called homeroom teachers; they're called "chief mentors".) Age unknown; he was a middle-aged man with black-rimmed glasses. In my impression, he was a stern teacher, and I was very afraid of him. Fortunately he didn't teach us in fifth grade — but when sixth grade came, because grades 3 and 4 were a paired class group, he was assigned as our math teacher, too.

I remember once in sixth grade I had an unexpected stellar showing and did better than usual. He called me out, grabbed me by the collar of my jacket, dragged me to the boys' toilet's washstand, and demanded:

"So you CAN score well, huh?! Huh?! And what did that score you gave me before mean?! Talk!"

At the Normal University-Affiliate school, when a teacher interrogated me, I couldn't and didn't dare say a word. But here, I was required to answer an interrogation; otherwise it was disrespecting the teacher. Later I found that in China, any superior demands this of subordinates — which left me especially unskilled at it. Because when I heard that tone of voice, I was already scared stiff, to the point of nearly crying. Sometimes the teacher would deliberately keep me there because I said nothing — which made me desperately afraid.

This man was no simple case. Rumor had it he was the then-principal's child, getting his positions as math teacher + grade director through connections. Rumors said the Class 5 math teacher even had to make his slides and script for his classes. Later in middle school the principal changed, and he left with the job — opening a tutoring class outside. During our high-school entrance exam, some classmates went to his class for final sprinting. The last time I saw him was on exam day, at the exam-site entrance, standing outside.

Sister Ying

She was my math teacher and our class's chief mentor, teaching me all of fifth grade's math. She came from the same county town as me.

She wasn't chief mentor from day one: first a middle-school teacher came to teach us math, transferred away within days; then the Class 1 teacher taught us a lesson or two; finally Sister Ying joined and taught us math.

That was probably the happiest stretch of my elementary years. Sister Ying was gentle, taught carefully — the kind of teacher who truly understands children. Most importantly, she never interrogated me in a towering rage. Even when I made mistakes, she used a soft tone.

One day I came to class late. When she asked why, I suddenly felt dizzy — nothing serious, honestly — but she still sent me to the infirmary, then took me to the office to rest. Brother Quan was in the office; fearing I'd be scared, she settled me outside and told me not to look at Brother Quan. Then she went back to her work. Once I'd recovered a bit, I went back to class.

Another day I forgot my schoolbag on the way to school — to me, a capital offense. One day in the Normal University-Affiliate school, without a bag, I'd been stopped by security. But she didn't lose her temper as I imagined. Although she was on the whole a strict teacher, in my memory there's no such scene of her at all.

Dare to Duck Round with Me?

I forget when this was — maybe sixth grade or seventh grade. One night at home, unable to sleep on my side, I suddenly had the thought of wearing a skirt. But as the eldest son, if there was a skirt in the house it would either be my mother's or my little sister's. Mom's was too big; my sister's, too small.

Still, I got up, off the bed, went into the next room's dressing area, and finally found the skirt my sister had worn during some Chinese New Year of a year unknown.

I stood before the mirror, held the skirt up in front of me for a try... then immediately put it back and returned to my room.

Not because I feared being discovered — but because I disgusted myself.

Middle School, and That Teacher

One day in the second semester of sixth grade, going upstairs back to the dormitory, a teacher suddenly called my name from behind. I thought: who is this, how do they know my name? Turning around, it took me three or four seconds to recognize the teacher who had interviewed me. If you've forgotten him, I mentioned him in the #Transfers section. After a greeting, I didn't think much more of it.

Entering middle school, I walked into the classroom with trepidation — and there he was, talking with some parents. Yes: he was my middle school's chief mentor. And he taught me for all three years.

We called him Brother Xian.

Brother Xian

Brother Xian was much more intense than Brother Quan. Brother Quan at worst pinched your skin — mostly scaring you. But Brother Xian would really put his hands on you...

He also taught politics to the whole grade. He was a Party member. Though strict and frightening, he was also a reasonable man, with his own moral code.

In seventh grade, a classmate was merely playing with his phone in the dorm. The dorm manager found it and turned him in. Brother Xian beat him up. The beating happened outside; we were in the classroom, and every hit made everyone's heart leap. He smashed the phone with no mercy at all. Whether that classmate later paid compensation, I never learned.

"Collective"?

The collectivism so many people hate today ran through my middle school years. For a short period, after our afternoon nap, we had to stand and sing the class song. What the "class song" was I've forgotten; I only remember it was quite an old song, with lyrics about collectivism or friendship.

One day we sang poorly — not loud enough, I think — so we were ordered to stand as punishment the whole afternoon.

That day the first class was physics, and we went to the lab. The teacher told us to sit. The others didn't sit. Only I sat.

After class I put my things away and went out to the toilet. When I came back, Brother Xian was already waiting at the door. Before I could even react, a force kicked me from behind to the ground. My mind went entirely blank.

Brother Xian: "Why did you sit down?! No one else sat but you sat?! Why are you SO special?! Speak!" Me: "The physics teacher... told us to sit..." Brother Xian: "You listen to anyone's word, don't you?! What right do you have, huh?! I'm telling you: besides MY words, you don't need to listen to anyone. Even if the principal comes, he listens to me!"

I got beaten. Then he let the others sit, and made me and one other stand for the whole afternoon...

"I'm telling you: besides MY words, you don't need to listen to anyone. Even if the principal comes, he listens to me!"

Growth Diary

At this school you had to write a "growth diary" — primary, middle, and high school all required it.

To be specific, the growth diary is: "a paperbound volume that the school — or the education group — forcibly requires every student to write in daily, in order to serve their so-called certain 'education models'".

Though named a "diary", the school required you to write tomorrow's plan — like a paper-based ToDo list.

Usually the diary has a fixed format, depending on different leaders' requirements and different periods. For example, the first two lines asked for the morning-reading recitation plan — precise to which hours, what to recite, which page of the textbook, to what degree of mastery (how "well-done"). If you missed a day's plan, you'd be required to make it up. Even if the morning-reading period had already passed, you still had to write the so-called "plan".

I hated writing it intensely. As long as no one checked mine, I left it blank. By the second half of the semester, I had quite a lot of blanks. That was when the teacher, to face the supervision inspection, basically chose to staple the unwritten parts up and had me symbolically write a few — and that was that.

Supervision

The school belonged to an education group; the group generally sent people to every school for a check in the first part of the semester and the last part. These people formed a department called the "Supervision Team".

From the school down to every small group, periodic or irregular checks of subordinate departments' functioning — partly to keep the school running normally, and partly to handle the two supervision inspections. Utterly absurd.

Rui

That was my good friend. Whenever there was a gathering or a comic convention, I'd invite him along. Later, though, his free time became fully booked; after I transferred schools I rarely saw him again.

We probably met in seventh grade. In my memory, the beginning of seventh grade we got along decently; later we hardly spoke; then we got along again.

Little Horse and the Piano

Little Horse was a boy from another class I got on well with in seventh grade. He loved playing the piano. I knew a bit of piano back then, learned over a summer — honestly, I could only play "Castle in the Sky". I never played it again, and Little Horse transferred schools too.

ZTZJ

She was the first girl I ever liked. Even now about all that's left are memories I can't bear to look at.

I still remember my first love letter: I didn't dare give it myself, and had someone else give it to her. What was I thinking then?

Sometimes when my finger or something got nicked and bled a little, I'd write love words in blood. (Which she never got.)

Now that I think about it, how different am I today?

When I first learned online shopping, I bought a few pocket watches; I gave one to her. When I had it customized, I even put her photo on the back cover.

The Boy Who Couldn't Sit at a Table

Around seventh grade, the only friend I had in the entire class was Rui. Our class had three tables assigned in the cafeteria, and everyone had the habit of clustering — so I got squeezed out of two tables. The third table was where the girls clustered; going there would probably get me called a pervert ().

Fortunately, I had some classmates in other classes with whom I wasn't on bad terms, so I went to eat at their tables. But the good times were short — the other classes' chief mentors gradually forbade class-hopping for meals (seemingly... aimed at me).

Several times I had absolutely nowhere to sit. I leaned against the railing by the stairs watching the evening news; if I didn't want to look too awkward, I'd go get a second serving of food. Eventually I even found a trick: if today's food was hard to grab, I'd rush in, get a portion, and see if there were free seats; if not, I'd fake a second serving until a seat opened. If the food was mediocre, I'd wait until later to eat.

First Attempt at Buying Women's Clothes?

I learned online shopping in middle school and tried buying little things — an Air China badge, a few refined pocket watches, one of which I gave to ZTZJ.

Later I used Pinduoduo to buy a JK uniform — pink. When it arrived, I dashed to my room and put it on.

That was my first time wearing women's clothes. I wasn't used to it; it felt drafty down there.

The car back to school was almost here, and I didn't have much time. Unwillingly, I hurriedly changed and went downstairs.

Lost

Later I wore it once more. Though not fully used to it, I loved it.

This time, after hiding it away, I never found it again.

I searched every possible place — nothing.

The nanny had no reason to steal; my brother and sister had no interest. In the end there was only one possibility: my parents discovered it.

A Second Outfit and the First Time Out

Actually, I had gone out in women's clothes quite early — just as cosplay, going with Rui to a convention.

I bought a uniform of Hoshino Takanashi plus a wig (I really couldn't afford make-up costs then, so the wig covered it). I went to the destination city a day early and booked a hotel. The next day, dressed in the cosplay outfit, I went to the convention and found Rui and his mother (I quite envy his mother, honestly — seeing me in a skirt she only asked, "Is this one of those Japanese school uniforms?", without pressing further).

WARNING: the expanded content contains heavy/graphic content; open with care.

Something happened while I was staying at the hotel — click here to view

That night I got into bed and suddenly felt something wet beneath my legs. Throwing off the covers, I found solid excreta left on the sheet by the previous guest. I instantly felt sick and immediately called the front desk to deal with it.

### Year One of High School

Shaken but unhurt, I entered high school — then came the most willful period of my student life.

My first-year homeroom teacher was a history teacher. Perhaps his teaching career wasn't perfect, but he truly taught me many things about being a person.

Once on my way home from school, I borrowed a phone charger from him. I finished using it, then left it on the charging cabinet. When I came back on the weekend, the charger had vanished into thin air. I checked the surveillance video for a long time and still couldn't find who stole it.

The teacher asked me to compensate. Unfortunately I didn't have much allowance then, and my allowance management was still fairly strict. In the end I chose to bear it alone. Thinking back: I lost nothing — instead it was the heaviest, most valuable lesson of my life, more useful than any other form.

Year Two of High School

In year one, I chose Japanese for my electives, and the idea of going to Japan for further study sprouted. So in year two, I transferred schools again, to Qingdao.

Management was indeed looser — but it came with all kinds of discrimination and all kinds of "gods". Including but not limited to: discrimination against Genshin Impact players, household-registration suppression, political disputes, discrimination over the shape of people's heads, discrimination against Arcaea (舞萌/maimai) players, and abstract people like "the Japanese guy only at N4 level".

Surviving here required technique; one small slip made you the joke of the whole class, even the whole school.

Year Three and the Last September

Strictly speaking, I didn't attend school. Because of the year-two god-people environment, I went back to Weifang and studied at a Japanese study-abroad agency. But that stretch didn't last long either...

Blown Out of the Closet

I disappeared online for a while. That night (September 30, Minguo 114 / 2025), half an hour after this post was published, I was blown out of the closet. My parents cursed at me for over an hour.

Sent to a Conversion Institution

Four days after being blown out of the closet (October 3), I slept until about 11 in the morning. My parents called me to eat — western food.

Nothing unusual about the day, but the dishes they ordered were exceptionally abundant. I grew alert.

After the meal they took us to my grandfather's house; said they wanted to take me to meet a relative, and left my brother and sister there.

There was no relative to meet. That was their lie. In reality I was sent to the worst place conceivable:

A conversion institution.

I have kept all the materials from that place, compiled at: Torsion.

This hit me extremely hard. Life inside was endless drills, scolding, and brainwashing. Now I cannot even imagine how I endured it back then. I always felt I was one step from collapse — one more step...

Master

She was a very cute little girl with an unfortunate lot in life. She was my classmate in the conversion institution. Her, actually, bore much of my pressure.

During that period we passed notes to each other constantly. Those written messages were probably the only words we could truly trust... We passed notes so often that even the instructors suspected we were dating.

Where Is This?

After leaving the internet-addiction school, all this happened to me

Running Away

I started preparing on February 11, before the conversion institution's holiday. Scraping together bits and pieces, I found just over 500 yuan — enough to barely pay for the February 14 Weifang–Shanghai Hongqiao train ticket. I went, without knowing whether my living would hold up there. X post

The letter I wrote my parents as the train left Shandong Province:

Ever since I went to Heart Seed, I've become an actor. Everything — performed for everyone around me.
Things were not so good as imagined...
Set aside the gender identity part: the day you sent me there, my trust in you shattered.
I no longer believe a single word — so much so that late one night, passing a motorcyclist, I thought my father was spying on me...
I cannot bear it.
I had this plan ready from the start.
I don't hate you...
No need for that
But one thing and another: because of this, I've developed a fear of all of Shandong.
I love you
This is not abandonment... just a sulk...
Everyone says everything I have is given by my parents...
Says I can't keep wealth past three generations...
Fine
I'll do it myself
Whatever the outcome
I can have an achievement...
I'm just telling you through my actions:
I am not useless — and conversion institutions are my red line.

Don't forget how many families this industry has destroyed.

KaKuKawa, February 14, 2026

When they learned I had left them, they sent many messages — whether truly ashamed or performing, I don't know. In any case, I bit back my guilt and kept reminding myself I could not go back. My emotions got a bit out of control, producing this passage:

So have I... run away from home...?
I know deep down the real perpetrator is the conversion institution...
Yet it looks like I'm the rebellious, runaway bad kid...
My parents just didn't want me to eat "sugar" (take HRT)...
They didn't try to stop me once they learned I'd escaped.
I was locked in a conversion institution for 4 months, living every day like a spy — yet I'd already escaped during that time!
So why do I still act like this, meow.....
Why
What about the family...
What I abandoned was everything...
Cao Yongwang! Aren't you the one who came to save families?! What have you saved?!

Or... am I just too hypocritical...?

Creating NO CONVERSION THERAPY

I had this idea not long after I was taken to the conversion institution, and once I reached Shanghai I turned it into reality step by step — powered by enormous energy, mixed with hate.

I didn't pin much hope on it, but in a let-me-try mood, I published the site: https://nct.hosinoneko.me

As of April 3, 2026, the site has collected more than a hundred testimonies, thanks to spreading within the community and traffic from Mu Yuan. It has become the project I'm proudest of.

Homelessing

The good times didn't last. On April 15, 2026 — a period when I was showing my father around Shanghai — there was a knock at the door in the morning. Police.

My website had caught their eye.

Beyond that, the friend who had been sheltering me also received a summons from the relevant authorities. That decision over there was even more severe.

I was ordered not to stay overnight in Minhang.

That was serious. Came within a hair's breadth of sleeping on the street twice: once the very same day (someone on Telegram offered me temporary lodging), and once after they could no longer take me in for some reason (on that occasion I received aid through X again).

Going Home

I've forgotten the exact time; I only know there was still an unbridgeable gap with my parents.

That day the Shanghai side demanded I return to Shandong — and I still carried a good deal of fear about returning there. The next evening, I bought a ticket to Guangdong, wanting to go there instead. Unfortunately, my PTSD flared — or more precisely, got triggered by the tone of the phone call.

To be continued...

By: HosinoNeko

title: Hope None of Us Has to Leave Again
contentHtml: I hope none of us ever has to leave again.

title: Tenacity That Roots Deep Into the Ground
contentHtml: No matter what caused your gender identity to differ or feel unclear, you must keep your own will tenacious. I recommend choosing to be open only after you've achieved financial independence and sufficient ability to withstand pressure — otherwise it's easy to develop psychological problems from stress and discrimination. If your family doesn't support or won't allow it, then endure and lie low. Don't fantasize that they'll suddenly accept it one day; don't depend on them long-term either. Through study or learning a trade, get as far away from the source of trouble as you can — the farther the better. Finally: don't OD, don't go into sex work, don't overuse hormone medications, and please don't harm yourself. Don't trust certain people on Twitter or in other communities who might push you into hurting yourself, and don't wallow in self-despair. No difficulty is unsurvivable — grit your teeth and you will get through. Trust me: as a former exam student from the "Four Mountain-Hard Provinces", I made it through too, and I'm doing fairly well now.

title: A Journey of Watching Each Other's Backs
contentHtml: Fight for all the beauty in the world! A while ago, I got my first ever hormone panel test. A sister took me there — we both got tested — and she gave me a little bead bracelet. I was so happy; it felt warm. Later I put the bracelet in my pencil case, took it with me to school — it's become my lucky charm, w. Meeting peers face-to-face is the most relaxed and pleasant kind of offline socializing there is, but it also often makes my chest ache — accompanied by a certain warm feeling... I've genuinely been helped a great deal by the offline mutual-aid actions of trans women. I hope everyone can actively build mutual-aid communities. — akizakura

title: The Wine-Soaked Needle, the Spirit Healer, and an Absurd Obsession
contentHtml:
Out of despair, I once came out with a nothing-to-lose attitude, then went back deep in the closet. I'm hoping to gain semi-independence (university) as soon as possible, to avoid the risk of conversion treatment. During the coming-out period, my parents sought help from relatives — a way out — and then took me almost a hundred kilometers to see a "magic immortal" (folk healer). The "immortal" had my mother soak a needle in wine and place it in my room, with a bowl of water beside it; the next morning I was to drink that bowl of water, and gather the needle to show him later. He wanted us to do this for three days, then stop two days, then repeat for three days.

Under the inducement of a "hospital broker" (medical tour guide), my parents took me to a private hospital for psychiatric evaluation, aiming to "cure" me (I'm actually grateful to that broker — otherwise the evaluation would never have happened; before this I believed I was unworthy of and couldn't possibly have an evaluation). Afterwards, my parents — holding the report showing severe OCD, moderate depression, and moderate anxiety — insisted I had nothing wrong, and went home disappointed that I hadn't been "cured". At the time they refused injection treatment and said: "A good beating will fix you."

Both of them dropped out of middle school. We're from a rural area in Northeast China. My father started construction work at 17 and did it all his life; my mother joined him working when I was in sixth grade. Since then I've mostly been looked after by my maternal grandmother (my paternal grandparents have passed). I once thought about running away, but didn't — because of all the restrictions society places on minors (afraid I couldn't survive). Currently I plan to endure at least until university, when I reach a semi-independent state; if my parents still object, I'll leave the family then.

title: Hope the World Is More Inclusive
contentHtml: I hope the world is more inclusive, and I hope all my friends going through gender dysphoria find their inner self soon 🥰🥰🥰 — be happy every day!

title: Survive the Long Night, and You'll See the Dawn
contentHtml: A few years ago I also thought I'd never make it to the next day — that life was meaningless. Later, I slowly adjusted my mindset and gritted through. Now, looking back at that period, it was unbearably bitter. But every effort gets repaid, so never give up — hold on, and you'll surely see the dawn.

title: Rain Stops — Sheathe the Umbrella as a Sword
contentHtml: I'm ftm, attracted to women. My earliest memory at age three is a gentle, beautiful older sister I met in the hospital, where I was sick. As a baby I showed unusual attachment to breasts. Since childhood, my personality and interests were masculine; my friends were mostly boys. In middle school I realized I was transgender. Severe depression ran through my entire adolescence; my family didn't accept it. Being clever and hard-working, I got into a 985 university and gradually walked out of the depression. Once I chatted with a French person, who described what it's like to be transgender in France — not being oppressed and discriminated against as in China. Transgender has brought me much trauma, and much gain. Just... living.

title: The Spectrum Beyond the Binary
contentHtml: I want people to understand that gender is not simply male or female. In this world, some people's gender differentiation naturally falls into neither category. We are a third gender — existing naturally, not subject to ideological shifts. As a group that cannot easily do ordinary manual labour like most people, and who must retreat from the public eye, we need to unite to win empowerment opportunities, contributing more technical and artistic value. The "effeminate man" carries half the sky: reject the sissy stereotype forced on us by the far right.

title: May the Other Babies Be Happier
contentHtml: I will never harm anyone but myself. May all the other "yaoniang" (trans women on hormones) babies be a little happier.

title: Finding a Corner to Live Quietly at the Heart of the City's Splendor
contentHtml: Words to the world: even in a first-tier city, a discordant family will affect a child for their whole life. A child longs so much for a harmonious family — it's too hard, and it has affected too much: studies, job hunting, the whole person has gone slack. I only wish for a good life, to happily be myself.

title: The Resonant Tuning Fork and the Sprouting Branch
contentHtml:
Actually, it's only the beautification of facts that counts as true instigation and propaganda. Seeing someone share OD and self-harm doesn't bother me — it's a way of venting that hurts no one else. Not expressing emotions not only fails to reduce the negative impact of "emotional contagion", it can actually intensify the feelings and cause us to miss the window for outside help. And there's no need to compare who's better — doing what you love is what matters most, what has meaning.

Reminder: drug abuse and self-harm can cause serious physical and psychological damage; please do not attempt or imitate. If you or someone around you is facing such distress, contact professional institutions for help in time.

contentHtml: But honestly I'm in so much pain, so much pain 😣 I yearn desperately to become a girl, or to become a transgender person who is respected. I want to cry. I long to be loved — so much, so much.

title: Want a Big Long Sleep, Want a Good Meal
contentHtml: Ugh, so tired. Want to sleep for ages. Want tasty food. Want to get rich. Want to do whatever I please.

title: The Sliver of Sunshine I Met at the Pizza Stall
contentHtml: While studying abroad in the UK, I met my favourite junior at the school's pizza stall — still my best sister to this day. She came out last year as ftm nonbinary. I hope I can keep guarding him as his big sister, w.

title: The Answer Quietly Budding Amid the Sneers
contentHtml: Because my personality was close to a girl's, I got mocked in elementary school for "being a girl". At that time my gender exploration was just sprouting; hearing those words, I didn't feel mocked at all — I even felt a little comfortable. Back then I didn't know I was MtF.

contentHtml: Blood for blood, fight heaven and earth, and never yield.

title: Skirts, Dolls, and the Late-Arriving Wholeness
contentHtml: Since childhood I've known I was different. Everyone said I looked like a girl, but no one thought I WAS a girl, and I also felt I should be with girls. I kept wondering what the difference between me and girls actually was. After learning, I've hated my genitals. I love skirts and dolls — but I had to force myself to like the things I believed boys should like. That feeling was truly painful. But now I've let go of much of it, and my body is improving too.

Executive Summary

The survey recruited respondents through an online questionnaire and describes their self-reported experiences of identity awareness, everyday expression, medical needs, family relationships, campus experiences, employment circumstances, mental health, and social support. The summary below condenses the key findings and directions for action; full data and methods appear in later chapters.

Important note

The survey used non-probability sampling, and the sample is dominated by young respondents (43.5% aged 18–22). All results describe only the respondents of this survey and cannot be generalised to transgender and gender-diverse people across China. All "associations" or "correlations" are statistical and do not imply causality.

1.1 Key Findings

Sample characteristics

A notably young sample

Among respondents with a valid age answer (n=899), 43.5% were 18–22, 20.6% were 16–17, and 9.0% were 12–15; the three youngest age groups together accounted for 73.1%. Gender identity was diverse (women 70.3%, non-binary 28.3%, men 11.7%, still exploring 11.6% — multiple choice). Residence was concentrated in urban tiers: tier-1 and new tier-1 cities together 44.0%, tier-2 cities 17.1%, tier-3 and below plus county/town 29.6%, and overseas plus Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan 9.3%. The medical needs, family dependence, campus experiences, and economic circumstances in this report must be read against this young sample structure.

Identity awareness and expression

Aware early, expression constrained

More than 80% of respondents (84.8%) noticed their gender identity difference at or before age 17 (13–17: 36.5%; 7–12: 33.9%; before 6: 14.3%). However, only 16.8% could live fully in line with their gender identity; expression is heavily concentrated in online spaces (87.7%) and trusted friend circles (55.3%), while rates in formal settings such as family, school, healthcare, and employment are notably low (all ≤16%). Well-being distributions differ by expression status (Cramér's V=0.144, adjusted p<0.001).

Healthcare access and voice needs

HRT common, channels informal, barriers multiple

71.9% of respondents who answered the HRT-status question (n=859) are currently on HRT, and 14.6% want to start but have not. Among respondents reporting how they obtain HRT (n=716, multiple choice), online informal sellers account for 66.6%, while regular hospital/clinic prescriptions in China account for 29.3%. Medical barriers include family opposition (59.9%), cost burden (51.7%), fear of discrimination (40.0%), resource shortage (35.4%), and insufficient professional supply (33.6%). Those more satisfied with medical care tend to also report higher well-being (rho=0.370, adjusted p<0.001, n=855).

Monitoring gaps

Only 20.4% of respondents undergo regular HRT health checks; 28.7% would like to but have no access.

Widespread voice anxiety

65.8% of respondents find it difficult or impossible to use a satisfying voice, and 56.9% are dissatisfied with their current voice. Voice is a significant source of gender-expression pressure.

Family

Awareness is not support

36.6% came out voluntarily; 29.6% said their family does not know; 20.1% were outed passively. Among respondents whose families know (multiple choice), silence/avoidance 58.2%, blame/accusation 48.4%, non-understanding 48.4%, support/acceptance 25.3%. Currently 26.9% describe "completely unsupportive"; among the 312 respondents who directly reviewed family attitude change, 49.4% report improvement, 36.9% report no real change, and 13.8% report deterioration. Those with more family support also tend to report higher well-being (rho=0.321, adjusted p<0.001).

Family restrictions and violence

Among respondents answering the family restriction/violence question for the past year (n=474, multiple choice), 39.7% experienced verbal/psychological violence, 33.3% medical interference, 20.0% economic violence, and 14.3% physical violence. Family harm involves medical autonomy, economic control, freedom of movement, and bodily safety.

Campus environment

Negative experiences widespread, institutions absent

73.7% of respondents answering the campus-experience question (n=749, multiple choice) reported at least one clear negative experience: verbal discrimination/ridicule 49.3%, isolation by classmates 44.6%, being required to dress as their assigned sex 36.0%, physical harassment/violence 27.2%. Those reporting more negative campus experiences also tend to report more psychological distress (rho=0.149, adjusted p<0.001).

More than 70% of respondents report almost no support or only sporadic support at school; the share of schools with overall supportive environments is under 20%. School policies that explicitly cover gender diversity and are effectively implemented are extremely rare (5.6%). Those with more school support also tend to report higher well-being (rho=0.278, adjusted p<0.001).

Employment and economy

Concealment is a primary cost

Among respondents with work experience (n=267, multiple choice), 52.1% had to hide their identity because it was not disclosed, 36.7% had to maintain an expression inconsistent with their gender identity, 23.2% were questioned because their documents did not match their appearance, and 21.3% were rejected for a job due to gender expression. 50.5% believe their transgender identity negatively affected their financial situation (n=283).

Mental health and safety support

Distress widespread, pressure multi-layered, support insufficient

Nearly 90% of respondents (88.4%) experienced at least one high-frequency emotional distress in the past six months (frequent anxiety 61.8%, frequent depressive moods 61.1%, emotional turbulence 58.0%). Pressure sources involve gender identity/body anxiety (83.7%), schoolwork (59.6%), family (58.6%), finances (56.7%), public policy/public opinion (41.4%), and healthcare access (32.9%). 45.5% find it difficult to obtain psychological support.

Self-harm and suicide-related experiences widespread

68.2% have a history of self-harm (had it but stopped 47.8%, still engaging in it 20.4%). On suicide-related experiences, lifetime self-reports show ideation without attempt 51.3% and attempt 37.6%; under that question's classification, at least one category was reported by 88.9%. These figures are evidence of safety support needs, not evidence of danger posed by transgender identity, and should not be attributed to the identity itself.

Well-being skewed low

47.1% rate their overall well-being negatively (n=896); only 20.7% say they are fairly or very happy.

Documents and public space

Document difficulties alongside public services

Nearly half of relevant respondents (48.8%) encountered questioning or inappropriate treatment in public affairs at least occasionally in the past six months. Those who face more document difficulties also report more difficulties with public services (Cramér's V=0.173, adjusted p=0.013).

Only 14.7% can comfortably use public facilities matching their gender identity; 35.3% are forced to use facilities for their assigned sex; 25.8% try to find alternatives; 22.9% avoid using them whenever possible.

Harassment fairly common

71.3% report some form of harassment experience (n=855). 21.2% frequently experience gender stereotypes or verbal bias; 72.1% at least occasionally (n=900).

Social support and desire for change

Inner resilience and peer support are the main protective sources

Their own inner strength 59.9%, friends in the transgender community 49.4%, cisgender friends who understand them 39.4%. Family support ranks low (11.6%). Those with more support sources also tend to report higher well-being (rho=0.179, adjusted p<0.001). 12.7% still say they currently draw strength and support from none.

Desire for change broad and diverse

83.7% would like to change body characteristics, but desire for change in voice (68.3%), finances (65.3%), mental health (63.5%), legal documents (55.6%), and family relationships (50.2%) is equally common — all above half. 80.0% express a strong desire for change (strongly want 43.5% + somewhat want 36.5%).

1.2 Cross-chapter threads

01
A young and diverse sample, aware early, but severely constrained in everyday expression: formal settings (family, school, healthcare, employment) lack safe conditions for expression.
02
Healthcare, family, campus, employment, documents and public space form interwoven practical barriers: for example, family opposition is reported alongside barriers to healthcare access, economic support, and identity expression; document-mismatch difficulties also appear across employment, public affairs, and public facilities.
03
Psychological distress must be interpreted within multi-layered external pressures, not attributed to identity itself: reported pressure sources involve body, schoolwork, family, finances, and institutional environments; distress should be read alongside multi-layered pressure, insufficient support, and safety needs — and cannot establish causal direction.
04
Inner resilience and relational networks protect, but coverage is uneven: structural responsibility should not be shifted onto individual resilience; services must actively reach the groups with the least support.
05
Desire for change spans body, voice, finances, psychology, law, and social environment: this is not a single medical issue.

1.3 Directions for action

The directions below draw on the survey findings and are intended as reference for service providers, policy discussions, and community organisations — not finalized policies that have passed cost-benefit or feasibility review:

Medical services

  • Expand regular, affordable HRT assessment, prescription and follow-up services; integrate HRT health monitoring into the service chain.
  • Provide harm-reduction information during the transition period where formal services do not yet sufficiently cover.
  • Treat voice support as a standalone service: offer informed-consent, non-conversion-based training and referral.
  • Improve privacy protection and professional training in medical services.
  • Review potential accessibility barriers related to age and guardian-consent requirements, and explore institutional paths that balance individual autonomy, informed consent, and minor protection.

Family support

  • Provide long-term family education and support programmes that can be entered repeatedly.
  • Offer families accurate, non-pathologizing information that addresses misconceptions, traditional values, and social pressure.
  • Build low-threshold safety plans, legal and psychological referrals, and emergency economic support.

Schools

  • Explicitly include protection of gender identity and expression in anti-bullying policies.
  • Establish support mechanisms with accountable staff, confidential procedures, and complaint channels.
  • Provide professional training for teachers.
  • Gradually reduce social stereotypes through systematic gender education, and promote gender education for students and families.

Employment and economy

  • Drive inclusive redesign of recruitment, dress codes, document verification, name use, and anti-harassment processes.
  • Offer more flexible, privacy-respecting alternatives in identity-verification processes.

Mental health and safety support

  • Provide trauma-informed, non-pathologizing psychological services covering a range of distress, not a single diagnosis.
  • Build low-threshold crisis support and long-term psychological services.
  • In presentations of self-harm and suicide-related content, connect directly to support resources and handle the topic neutrally, without sensationalism.

Documents and public services

  • Simplify document-change procedures and improve accessibility; reform front-desk identity-verification processes.
  • Increase the supply of gender-neutral public facilities and push for gender-neutral redesign.

Social support and resource visibility

  • Expand peer networks, partner and family support, while respecting individual resilience without transferring responsibility onto individuals.
  • Make local support resources more visible and expand actual supply.
  • Proactively reach the groups with the least support.

Cross-cutting principles

  • Design support around diverse needs for change, covering body, voice, finances, psychology, law, and social environment.
  • Respect individual autonomy: respond to desire for change while respecting those who are unsure or do not want to change.

1.4 Research limitations

  • Non-probability sampling and a young sample restrict generalisation: the results cannot be generalised to all transgender and gender-diverse people in China.
  • Self-report and cross-sectional design limit interpretation: all data are self-reported and collected at a single point in time; associations are not used to infer temporal order or causality.
  • An unexamined item is not "no association"; an item short of adjusted significance is not "no relationship": some pre-specified tests may fall short due to sample size, measurement, or analysis limits.
  • Passing technical QA does not establish representativeness, validity, external validity, or scientific conclusions: technical QA only verifies the accuracy of numeric processing.
  • Reporting bias on sensitive topics: domestic violence, self-harm, and suicide content may be under- or over-reported.
  • Measurement limits of single items or multi-select proxies: some core concepts cannot capture all dimensions.

Full research limitations and methods are in Chapters 2 and 11.

1.5 How to read this report

  • This report has 12 chapters: Chapter 2 introduces methods and limitations; Chapters 3–10 present findings by domain; Chapter 11 synthesizes conclusions and directions for action; Chapter 12 provides the appendix.
  • Results already assigned a Result_ID can be checked against the public tracking table described in Appendix C for aggregate figures and calculation notes; FIG028–FIG033 are registered in Appendix A by Figure_ID, with their aggregation recomputation records currently retained in internal audit materials. None of the public materials can be used to trace individual responses.
  • This report recommends keeping three boundaries in mind: within-sample description, self-reported data, and statistical association.
  • Sensitive content (domestic violence, self-harm, suicide) is presented neutrally, without sensationalism or pathologization; relevant chapters provide psychological support and crisis-intervention resources (Chapters 8 and Appendix E).
Acknowledgements

We thank every respondent who shared their real experiences in the questionnaire. This report rests on respondents' self-reports and provides an empirical starting point for improving the situation of transgender and gender-diverse people. Improvement requires systemic collaboration across healthcare, family, education, employment, law, and social environment — and respect for each individual's autonomy and diverse needs.

Background, Sample Characteristics, and Methodological Boundaries

Barriers faced by transgender and gender-diverse people in healthcare access, family support, school environments, employment conditions, and public services have been widely documented in international literature. A cross-sectional study based on the Chengdu TREASURE cohort also reports a statistical association between traumatic experiences (including LGBTQ+-related adversity) and depressive symptoms, discussed within a framework of minority stress, social support, and coping (Yang et al., 2026; see Appendix F).

2.1 Background and purpose2.2 Sample characteristics2.3 Methods and research limitations2.4 Terminology2.5 Structure of the report

2.1 Background and purpose

This study uses a cross-sectional self-report questionnaire design and recruited respondents through online platforms. The survey covers age of identity awareness, expression settings, use and access to hormone replacement therapy (HRT), family awareness and support, campus and workplace experiences, mental health status, difficulties using public services and facilities, sources of social support, and willingness to change the status quo. The survey makes no clinical diagnosis; prior diagnosis experiences reported by respondents are self-reports, unverified against medical records. Other experiences are likewise unverified by physiological measurement or third-party checks.

2.2 Sample characteristics

2.2.1 Age distribution: a notably young sample

The sample is notably young; 18–22 is the largest age groupKey finding

Among respondents who answered the age question (n=899), the distribution shows a clear youth bias.

18–22 accounted for 43.5% (391 people), the largest age group; 16–17 for 20.6% (185 people); 12–15 for 9.0% (81 people). The three youngest age groups together accounted for 73.1% of respondents with a valid answer. 23–29 accounted for 23.2% (209 people), 30–39 for 3.4% (31 people), and the remaining low-frequency categories together 0.2% (2 people).

This age structure is directly related to the recruitment channels (mainly online social platforms and community networks) and the sample type (non-probability convenience sampling). The high share of young respondents means that the medical needs, family dependence, campus experiences, and economic circumstances described here must be read against this age backdrop. Topics in later chapters — family conflict, enrolment status, minors' medical decision rights, and economic autonomy — are closely tied to this age structure.

Reading note: the findings describe only the respondents of this survey and cannot be directly generalised to all transgender and gender-diverse people across China. All percentages use valid respondents to that question as the denominator; the number of valid respondents may differ between questions.

2.2.2 Diversity of gender identities

Gender identities in the sample are diverseKey finding

Among valid respondents to the gender-identity question (n=899, multi-select), women accounted for 70.3% (632 people), non-binary 28.3% (254 people), men 11.7% (105 people), still exploring 11.6% (104 people), genderfluid 10.1% (91 people), and agender 7.7% (69 people). Because this was a multi-select question, some respondents selected more than one category, so the percentages sum to more than 100%.

This distribution indicates clear diversity in gender identity among respondents: they should not be reduced to a single "transgender" category. When reading the medical needs, expression strategies, and support sources in later chapters, keep in mind that the experiences of people with different gender identities may differ. The analysis in this report is based on the records included in the main analysis and does not run formal statistical tests by gender-identity subgroup, so later findings should be read as overall patterns "among the respondents of this survey", not precise descriptions of a particular subgroup.

2.2.3 Residence: tier-1 and new tier-1 cities together largest share

Respondents live mainly in tier-1, new tier-1, and tier-2 citiesKey finding

Among respondents who answered the residence question (n=883 ), tier-1 cities (Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen) accounted for 22.3% (197 people), new tier-1 cities (Chengdu, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Nanjing, etc.) 21.9% (193 people), tier-2 cities 16.9% (149 people), tier-3 and below 19.0% (168 people), county towns or townships 10.6% (94 people), overseas 7.2% (64 people), and Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan regions of China 2.0% (18 people).

Tier-1 and new tier-1 cities together have the largest share, and tier-3-and-below plus county/town also has a meaningful share. This regional distribution is related to online recruitment channels and may run parallel to differences in medical resources, community activity, and information access across city tiers, providing context for barriers such as "no relevant medical resources in my area" in later chapters.

2.2.4 Descriptive subgroup stratification: age, gender identity, and HRT direction

To complement the overall results, this section stratifies descriptively along three confirmed dimensions: age into under 18 and 18 or above; gender identity into mutually exclusive groups of transfeminine/female identity, transmasculine/male identity, non-binary, and other/multiple; and HRT direction into feminizing and masculinizing per V036. The indicators are: currently on HRT, "want bottom/genital surgery but currently lack the conditions", and positive well-being ("fairly happy" or "very happy"). Each indicator uses valid respondents to that question within the group as its denominator; stratification is descriptive only — no significance tests or causal interpretation.

  • Age: among the under-18 group (n=266), 159/250 (63.6%) are currently on HRT; bottom/genital surgery "want but lack conditions" 98/148 (66.2%); positive well-being 42/265 (15.8%). 2.3 Methods and research limitations

2.3.1 Survey design

The survey used a structured online questionnaire distributed through Tencent Survey and Google Forms. Submission dates recoverable from the current workbook run from 2 June to 30 July 2026 (workbook local time; the project materials do not save a separate timezone note). The questionnaire contains closed-ended choice questions (single and multi-select) and ordered rating items, covering identity awareness, expression, healthcare, family, campus, employment, mental health, public services, and social support. The design drew on common frameworks of international transgender health surveys, with some wording and options adapted to the Chinese context.

Recruitment channels included transgender community social media accounts, online mutual-aid groups, social platforms of relevant non-profit organisations, and snowball forwarding by respondents. Participation was voluntary: the current questionnaire states the purpose, data-use approach, and privacy protections at the outset and requires confirmation of informed consent before proceeding. The project's surviving materials do not record formal inclusion criteria for recruits, minimum-age statements, or processes for minor respondents' own informed participation and guardian consent (or waiver), so this report cannot retroactively assume those processes; the age question does include a 12–15 option, and the sample includes respondents under 18. This material gap is listed as a research ethics and interpretation limitation.

2.3.2 Data processing

Raw questionnaire data were processed as follows:

1
Consent eligibility screening
4 submissions with explicit refusal and no subsequent valid answers were excluded. The old questionnaire produced 13 submissions: 1 recorded "willing" in the consent field, while the other 12 lacked a structured consent field; all 12 were completed and submitted, with no explicit refusal recorded, so the main analysis followed the old questionnaire's flow and treated continued completion as an expression of willingness to participate and included them.
2
Invalid entries and cross-platform duplicates
Apart from consent screening, no other record was excluded as "entirely invalid"; logic anomalies were excluded by affected variable. The only cross-platform duplicate pair was merged into one record — the primary version retained, the other filled in only blank fields — with 0 field conflicts verified.
3
Merging synonymous options
Because wording differed across time periods and platforms, some synonymous options were standardised and merged to ensure comparability.
4
Variable-level missing and logic exclusion
Valid respondents to each question are computed independently. Structural missingness, not-applicable skips, unanswered items, and logic conflicts are recorded separately; e.g. 1 record with an age logic conflict was excluded only from age analysis rather than removed from all analyses.

The main-analysis sample flow: 905 raw submissions; consent screening excluded 4 explicit refusals and kept 12 old-questionnaire submissions completed with no refusal; 901 source submissions remained; after merging 1 cross-platform duplicate, n=900 entered the main analysis; the age variable then excluded 1 logic conflict, valid n=899.

Sensitivity analysis: a stricter scope that kept only verifiable explicit consent records excluded the 12 old-questionnaire records, yielding analysis n=888 and valid age n=887. Comparing 353 Result_IDs cited in the text under the same scope, the maximum absolute difference in descriptive percentages was 0.55 percentage points; no flip from "adjusted p<0.05" occurred among the 23 completed pre-specified tests. The n=888 scope is used only to test sensitivity to the consent-handling choice and is not the main analysis. Full aggregation differences ship with the public package.

All figures in the text are copied from the main analysis results table and were not recomputed during report writing. The public package also provides an item-by-item aggregation tracking table listing chapter, indicator, denominator, counts, percentages, Result_ID, and calculation notes; readers may verify aggregate statistics but cannot and should not trace any individual response.

2.3.3 Statistical methods

Descriptive statistics mainly use frequencies, percentages, and medians for ordinal variables. Association tests use chi-square tests (categorical variables) or Spearman rank correlation (ordinal variables), reporting effect sizes (Cramér's V or Spearman's rho) and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values. All statistical tests are exploratory; adjusted p<0.05 is treated as statistically significant.

"Association" or "correlation" in this report means statistical association only, not causation. The cross-sectional design cannot establish temporal order or causal direction. Mental health, well-being, and support analyses are all based on self-report. The survey makes no clinical diagnosis; the prior-diagnosis question likewise records only self-reports, unverified against medical records. The psychological-status items are not a single validated clinical scale.

2.3.4 Research limitations

Non-probability sampling
Respondents were recruited voluntarily through online channels, not random sampling, so representativeness cannot be guaranteed. The results describe only the respondents of this survey and cannot be generalised to all transgender and gender-diverse people in China or to other countries and regions.

The study has the following important limitations, which readers should consider when interpreting results:

Young sample age structure
As noted in 2.2.1, respondents aged 18–22 hold the largest share (43.5%), while those 23 and above together account for 26.6% (23–29: 23.2%; 30–39: 3.4%). This age structure shapes the reading of medical needs, family dependence, campus experiences, employment circumstances, and financial conditions: younger respondents may more often be in school, dependent on family financial support, not yet in the labour market, or still in early stages of family conflict.
Self-reported data
All data are self-reported by respondents and unverified by third parties. Descriptions of emotional distress and mental health are based on subjective experience and are not clinical diagnoses. Reports of family reactions, campus experiences, and workplace discrimination reflect respondents' perception and memory, which may be affected by recall bias and personal interpretation.
Cross-sectional design
All data were collected at a single point in time, so temporal order or causality between variables cannot be established. For example, the statistical association between identity expression and well-being cannot determine whether expression affects well-being, whether well-being affects willingness to express, or whether both are influenced by third factors (e.g. family support, financial conditions).
Measurement instruments
Some concepts in the questionnaire (e.g. "family support", "school support", "well-being") are measured with single-item ordinal ratings or multi-select proxies that cannot capture every dimension of the concept. For instance, "family support" is measured by one rating item about overall feelings, without distinguishing emotional support, financial support, medical-decision support, and other layers.
Limits of interpretation of statistical associations
All "associations" or "correlations" passing statistical tests in this report are exploratory results, not preceded by sample-size calculations or effect-size estimation. An adjusted-significant p-value only indicates a statistical association observed in this sample; it does not imply truth in the population or substantive importance. Tests that fell short of adjusted significance (e.g. F024, F025, F026) cannot be read as "no association" — they may be limited by sample size, measurement instruments, or analytical methods.
Reporting bias on sensitive topics
Some questions touch on highly sensitive content such as domestic violence, self-harm, and suicide-related experiences. Respondents may under- or over-report out of privacy concerns, psychological defence, or worry about consequences. Choosing "no clear negative experience" or "never" cannot be inferred to mean complete absence of such experiences.
Limited historical comparison
The report's structure was informed by the 2021 national transgender health survey, but differences in questionnaire wording, recruitment channels, sample composition, and statistical methods mean the two surveys are not strictly comparable. This report performs no cross-year percentage comparison or trend inference.

2.3.5 Ethics and privacy

The survey followed these principles in design and implementation:

  • The current questionnaire requires reading and confirming the informed-consent statement before answering; the 12 old-questionnaire records lack a structured consent field but were all completed with no explicit refusal, so the main analysis treats continued completion under the old flow as willingness to participate, with sensitivity analysis under the strict explicit-consent scope n=888.
  • Data analysis in this report uses only the closed-question workbook. The analytic flow did not access or use contact fields; the separate workbook containing contact information or open-text content did not enter the analysis. Public report and analysis artefacts contain no raw contact information, open-text originals, raw record IDs, or information directly identifying individuals.
  • The surviving project materials contain no verifiable institutional ethics-review documents, minimum-age rules, or records of minor participation/guardian consent (or waiver). This is not to assert that the project was never reviewed, but to explain that the public report cannot confirm it from available evidence; the report lists this as an explicit limitation and does not substitute technical QA for ethics review.
  • Where verifiable materials are insufficient, data-minimisation and alternative protections at the analysis stage include: read-only raw inputs, isolation of contact information and open-text answers, aggregate-only reporting, merging of low-frequency categories, neutral language for sensitive content, and provision of crisis-support resources.
  • Presentations of sensitive content — self-harm, suicide, domestic violence — use neutral, non-sensational, non-pathologizing language, and relevant chapters list contact details for psychological support and crisis-intervention resources.

2.4 Terminology

For ease of reading, the report defines the following core terms:

  • Transgender: people whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth. In this report "transgender" is used broadly, covering trans women, trans men, and other people whose gender identity does not fit the binary framework.
  • Gender diverse: including but not limited to transgender, non-binary, genderfluid, agender, and other gender identities.
  • Sex assigned at birth: the sex assigned at birth based on physical characteristics, usually "male" or "female".
  • Gender identity: an individual's inner sense and experience of their own gender.
  • Gender expression: external presentation of gender through clothing, behaviour, manner, voice, and the like.
  • Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT): medical measures using hormonal medication to move secondary sex characteristics toward the recognized gender. In this report "HRT" covers feminizing HRT (oestrogen and anti-androgens) and masculinizing HRT (testosterone).
  • Gender affirmation: the umbrella of medical, social, and legal measures supporting an individual to live in line with their gender identity, including but not limited to HRT, surgery, document changes, and social support.
  • Coming out: voluntarily disclosing one's transgender identity to others. This report distinguishes "voluntary coming out" from "passive coming out / passive discovery".
  • Cisgender: people whose gender identity matches the sex assigned at birth.
