3.1 Age of gender-identity awareness

Many respondents began to notice their gender identity difference in childhood or adolescenceKey finding

Among respondents who answered the awareness-age question (n=899), quite a few became aware early that their gender identity did not match their sex assigned at birth.

36.5% (328 people) became aware at 13–17, 33.9% (305 people) at 7–12, and 14.3% (129 people) before age 6. These three early stages together account for 84.8% of all valid respondents. Those who became aware at 18–22 account for 7.7% (69 people), still exploring 3.6% (32 people), uncertain/don't remember 2.6% (23 people), and after age 23 1.4% (13 people).

This finding suggests that gender-identity awareness often emerges while family and school still shape daily life heavily. For individuals who became aware in childhood or early adolescence, family reactions, school inclusivity, and age-appropriate information and support become especially critical. Note also that these data rest on retrospective self-reports, which may be affected by memory bias, and do not represent the awareness-age distribution of all transgender and gender-diverse people.

Reading note: the awareness-age distribution is related to this sample's age structure. As described in Chapter 2, the sample is dominated by respondents aged 18–22 (43.5%); younger respondents are closer in time to their awareness point, so recall may be clearer, but they may also be more likely to attribute awareness to a specific age band.

3.2 Identity-expression status and settings

3.2.1 Overall status of identity expression

Fully living as one's gender identity is not common; expression status and well-being are statistically associatedKey finding

Among respondents who answered the expression-status question (n=876), the share able to live fully as their gender identity is not high.

42.8% (375 people) can live as their gender identity only in some settings, 20.9% (183 people) only online, 16.8% (147 people) fully, 15.6% (137 people) almost never, and 3.9% (34 people) not at all.

Combining "almost never" and "not at all", nearly 20% of respondents can barely express their gender identity in daily life. Combining "only online" and "some settings", more than 60% of respondents face clear setting-based limits on expression.

Well-being distributions differ by expression status. The two are statistically associated (Cramér's V=0.144, adjusted p<0.001, n=872).

Among these respondents, those able to live as their gender identity in more settings differ from those whose expression is constrained. However, family support, financial conditions, and social environment may also influence both expression and well-being.

The questionnaire records identity expression and well-being over the same period; it cannot determine which came first, nor prove that fuller expression directly raises well-being.

3.2.2 Settings where respondents can express their gender identity

Online spaces and friend networks carry identity expression; formal settings fall clearly shortKey finding

Among respondents who answered the expression-settings question (n=579, multi-select), identity expression is heavily concentrated in informal settings.

Online socializing/online identity 87.7% (508 people), friend or acquaintance circles 55.3% (320 people). By contrast, expression in formal settings is clearly lower: public space 27.8% (161 people), school 15.5% (90 people), in front of family/relatives 13.5% (78 people), healthcare 13.3% (77 people), and work/job-hunting only 6.9% (40 people).

Possible mechanisms / interpretive discussion (not directly measured by this question): this pattern suggests that informal support networks (online socializing and trusted friend circles) provide relatively usable expression space, while gaps in formal settings — family, school, healthcare, employment — are more pronounced. The high online share may relate to anonymity, selectivity, and the community's online clustering, but it also reflects insufficient support in offline formal settings. These mechanism explanations draw on community experience and existing research and cannot be treated as direct measurements from this question.

Reading note: this was a multi-select question, so percentages sum to more than 100%. It was open only to respondents able to express themselves "in some settings" (n=579), excluding those who "almost cannot" or "cannot at all" — so results cannot be compared directly as percentages against all records in the main analysis (n=900).

3.3 How and how widely identity is disclosed

3.3.1 The layered nature of disclosure

Disclosure mostly happens within a few trusted relationships and online spacesKey finding

Among respondents who answered the disclosure-audience question (n=900, multi-select), disclosure is clearly stratified. Telling a few trusted friends 62.8% (565 people), only online 39.6% (356 people), telling family (voluntary coming out) 32.9% (296 people). By contrast, disclosure to wider groups is rarer: passively exposed due to physical changes or other reasons ("blown out of the closet") 11.1% (100 people), fully hidden 9.0% (81 people), disclosed at school/workplace 7.7% (69 people), and fully open 6.8% (61 people).

This distribution shows that disclosure is not a binary "out or not" state but a contextual, layered process. Most respondents selectively disclose to trusted individuals or small groups rather than to all social relationships. The high online share matches F004 and underscores the role of online space in expression and community connection.

3.3.2 Passive exposure and continued concealment

Passive exposure and full concealment are both real identity-management experiencesKey finding

Besides voluntary disclosure, some respondents experienced passive exposure or chose continued concealment. In the disclosure-audience question (n=900, multi-select), 9.0% (81 people) chose "not disclosed to anyone at all" and 11.1% (100 people) reported passive exposure ("blown out of the closet") due to physical changes or other reasons; 5.7% (51 people) do not voluntarily disclose at school/workplace but may be detected. In the supplementary passive-exposure options, 4.3% (39 people) reported passive exposure.

Possible mechanisms / interpretive discussion (not directly measured by this question): passive exposure (having one's identity disclosed by others without consent) can bring safety risks, broken relationships, or forced encounters with unprepared reactions. Continued concealment may carry long-term psychological costs, limited expression, and the strain of maintaining a double identity in social interaction. These mechanisms draw on community experience and existing research; they cannot be treated as direct measurements from this question.

Reading note: the percentages above come from different question versions and options and cannot be directly summed or compared. "Passive exposure" and "continued concealment" may co-occur in the same person (e.g. exposed once, then worked to re-conceal).

3.4 Identity expression and other experiences

3.4.1 Expression and negative campus experiences

The pre-specified test between expression and negative campus experiences fell short of adjusted significanceKey finding

This analysis found no clear statistical association between identity-expression status and negative campus experiences (Cramér's V=0.108, adjusted p=0.118, n=729).

This does not mean expression and campus experience are unrelated. Expression is recorded with a single five-level item, and campus negative experiences are compressed into a simplified indicator, which may miss specific settings, frequency, and severity. These data can only show that evidence is not yet clear-cut; they cannot prove "no relationship".

This finding also implies that even among respondents able to express their gender identity fully, negative campus experiences may still occur for other reasons — expression not matching stereotypes, being seen as "not masculine/feminine enough", or simply because of transgender identity itself. Campus support must cover all gender-diverse students, not only those "unable to express".

3.4.2 Attraction and exploration

Attraction is diverse; pansexual and femininity-oriented attraction are relatively commonKey finding

Among respondents who answered the attraction question (n=878 , multi-select), women/femininity 49.2% (432 people), everyone (pansexual) 34.2% (300 people), men/masculinity 27.4% (241 people), non-binary/genderfluid people 24.5% (215 people), still exploring 21.6% (190 people), and attracted to no gender (asexual) 8.5% (75 people).

This distribution indicates attraction is not concentrated on a single gender expression; a fair share report pansexual (33.8% ) or still exploring (21.7% ). This diversity suggests support services and community discussions should not assume a single attraction pattern — identity expression and intimate relationships are likewise diverse.

3.5 Chapter summary

The findings in this chapter sketch a complex picture of identity awareness, disclosure, and expression:

  1. Early awareness: more than 80% of respondents noticed their gender identity difference at or before age 17; family and school reactions during this period are crucial for individual development.

  2. Constrained expression: the share living fully as their gender identity is not high (16.8%), and over 60% face clear setting-based limits. Well-being distributions differ by expression status — a link, not proof of causation.

  3. Setting divergence: online spaces and trusted friend circles are the main settings for expression (87.7% and 55.3%), while formal settings — family, school, healthcare, employment — are clearly lower (all ≤16%).

  4. Layered disclosure: disclosure is stratified; most respondents selectively disclose to close friends, online communities, and a few family members rather than to all social relationships.

  5. Privacy risks: passive exposure and continued concealment are both real identity-management experiences; support for privacy protection and safe expression must cover voluntary disclosure, passive exposure, and continued concealment alike.

These findings suggest that supporting gender-diverse individuals' expression and disclosure requires more than "how to come out" information: it requires improving safety and inclusivity in formal settings — family, school, healthcare, workplace — while respecting each person's autonomy over the scope, timing, and manner of disclosure.

Later chapters present experiences in healthcare, family, campus, employment, and mental health, all of which are closely tied to the conditions and costs of identity expression.

4.2 HRT access channels

HRT access relies heavily on private and informal channels; formal medical coverage is limitedKey finding

Among respondents who answered the HRT-access question (n=716, multi-select), formal healthcare is not the main route.

Online private sellers 66.6% (477 people), the most common channel. Domestic formal hospital/clinic prescriptions 29.3% (210 people), domestic platforms/grey cross-border merchants (including disguised online sales like appointment mailing and private order-transfer) 28.6% (205 people), buying others' homemade products (e.g. homemade gels hawked within the community) 19.0% (136 people), overseas formal medical institutions 10.8% (77 people), and homemade products (homemade gels, homemade injections, etc.) 10.5% (75 people).

This distribution shows online private sellers are the most common channel. Among valid respondents on the cross-recomputed V038 question path (n=512), 35.4% (181 people) chose at least one of domestic formal hospital/clinic prescription or overseas formal medical institution, with 21 people choosing both; that union share cannot be obtained by adding 28.7% and 10.7% directly. Because this was a multi-select question, each percentage uses its own valid denominator. Use of e-commerce platforms, others' homemade products, and homemade products each falls in the 10%–30% range, suggesting that some respondents turn to less transparent channels of harder-to-guarantee quality and safety when formal healthcare is unavailable.

Reading note: this question merges HRT-access items across question versions; its specific paths and sample composition mean it is not open to all main-analysis records, so n=716 represents only valid respondents to this question, not all HRT users or all respondents. This report does not blame channel use on individual choice; it reads it as the result of insufficient accessibility and continuity of formal medical services.

4.2.1 Main sources of medical information: the wiki community is the most important

Medical information depends heavily on wikis and community; formal medical channels inform a limited shareKey finding

Among respondents who answered the information-source question (n=810, multi-select), MtF.wiki/FtM.wiki/RLE.wiki 45.7% (370 people), transgender communities (QQ groups, WeChat groups, etc.) 15.7% (127 people), social media (Twitter, Weibo, Xiaohongshu, etc.) 11.1% (90 people), AI tools 8.8% (71 people), doctors or professional consultation 6.9% (56 people), friends or other transgender people sharing 4.7% (38 people), and self-study of medical papers/clinical guidelines 4.6% (37 people).

Wikis are the leading source (45.7%), far ahead of transgender communities (15.7%) and social media (11.1%). Project Trans's wiki community plays a key role in this sample's medical literacy: it synthesizes procedures, risks, and cautions for HRT, surgery, diagnosis certificates, and related topics in a structured format, becoming the first stop for many respondents to obtain basic medical information when formal medical consultation is limited. The share citing doctors or professional consultation as an information source is only 6.9%, indicating limited formal involvement in information provision.

This distribution echoes 4.1: when formal channels under-cover information, community-maintained resources like wikis fill the gap. Support strategies could consider collaborating with wiki and community information sources to ensure accuracy and currency, while increasing formal channels' informational accessibility.

4.2.2 Medication-supply difficulties

Supply difficulties include high-premium purchasing, withdrawal reactions, and opaque order-transferKey finding

Among respondents who answered the supply-difficulty question (n=781, multi-select), forced to buy at a high premium on the black market 26.4% (206 people), severe physical or psychological reactions from running out of medication 19.2% (150 people), forced to switch to more opaque purchasing methods such as appointment mailing or private order-transfer 14.6% (114 people), defrauded by online sellers or dealers 8.2% (64 people), and bought counterfeit or ineffective medication 5.2% (41 people).

These experiences indicate that supply-channel instability and opacity sit alongside financial burden, withdrawal experiences, and medication predictability concerns. The questionnaire does not test causal paths between price, switches, withdrawal, and specific physical or psychological outcomes.

Reading note: the question stem mentions "policy changes or platform crackdowns", but the data cannot establish causality between policy and individual experience. These difficulties should be read within channel characteristics, supply chains, regulatory environments, and market behaviour; this survey cannot judge each factor's independent effect or causal direction.

4.2.3 Use of non-pharmaceutical-grade preparations and unconventional substitutes

Some feminizing-HRT respondents have used or still use non-pharmaceutical-grade preparations or unconventional substitutesKey finding

Among respondents who answered the unconventional-preparation question (n=731), 14.1% (103 people) used them before, 12.3% (90 people) still use them, and 73.6% (538 people) never used them.

Combining "used before" and "still using", 26.4% of respondents have experience with non-pharmaceutical-grade preparations or unconventional substitutes. This aligns with the access channels in F006 — others' homemade (19.0%) and homemade (10.5%) products — suggesting that when formal prescriptions are unavailable, private channels are unstable, or financial pressure is high, some respondents turn to less standardized alternatives.

This distribution should not be read as faulting individuals; it flags the accessibility gap in formal medical services as the issue to address. Responses include expanding affordable formal prescription and follow-up services, and providing harm-reduction information during the transition period where formal services do not yet cover, helping users understand risks of different preparations, how to spot quality problems, and when to seek care.

Reading note: this question did not ask preparation names, dosages, or usage, so specific risks or health harms cannot be inferred. "Used but stopped" may reflect switching to formal channels, financial reasons, side effects, or other personal considerations — one size does not fit all.

4.3 Barriers to healthcare

4.3.1 HRT-related spending and surgery intention

HRT-related spending is most commonly ¥100–300/month; about 20% report no current spendingKey finding

Among respondents answering the monthly HRT medication/check-up/related-spending question (n=545 ), ¥100–300/month 36.1% (197 people), no current spending 19.1% (104 people), ¥300–600/month 14.7% (80 people), ¥50–100/month 13.6% (74 people), unstable/hard to estimate 6.4% (35 people), below ¥50/month 5.9% (32 people), and ¥600–1000/month 2.8% (15 people).

After merging synonymous tiers across questionnaire versions by amount band, monthly spending clusters at ¥100–300; about 20% report no current spending. Gender-affirming surgery intention: "want bottom/genital reconstruction but lack conditions" is the largest category; completed rates are extremely lowKey finding

Among respondents answering the bottom/genital reconstruction (bottom surgery) intention question (n=582), want but currently lack conditions 60.3% (351 people), not planning 17.5% (102 people), planning/recent surgery 8.8% (51 people), uncertain 8.4% (49 people), and completed 4.6% (27 people).

For facial gender-affirming surgery (FFS/FMS) intention (n=572 ): want but currently lack conditions 54.9% (314 people), completed 1.0% (6 people). For chest surgery intention (n=563 ): want but currently lack conditions 40.3% (227 people), completed 0.9% (5 people).

For all three surgery types, "want but currently lack conditions" is the dominant category while "completed" is extremely low (≤4.6%). Together with the medical barriers in this section (cost burden 51.7% , family opposition 59.9% ), this shows a clear gap between surgery intention and accessibility: unmet needs extend beyond HRT to gender-affirming surgery.

Barriers come from family, cost, discrimination concerns, and resource shortage alikeKey finding

Among respondents who answered the medical-barriers question (n=806, multi-select), barriers show multiple sources.

Family not understanding or opposing 59.9% (483 people), cost burden too heavy 51.7% (417 people), fear of discrimination or exposure at hospitals 40.0% (322 people), no relevant medical resources in the area 35.4% (285 people), cannot find a doctor willing to provide services 33.6% (271 people), worried about side effects without professional guidance 26.2% (211 people), and lack of formal information channels 22.1% (178 people).

Family opposition (59.9%) and cost burden (51.7%) are the two most reported barriers, both above half. Discrimination concerns (40.0%), resource shortage (35.4%), and insufficient professional supply (33.6%) each sit around one third. This distribution calls for simultaneous attention to family relationships, economic conditions, institutional environments, regional resource distribution, and professional supply; the questionnaire cannot judge how layers interact or confirm causal direction.

Those more satisfied with medical care tend to also report higher overall well-being. The association is comparatively clear (Spearman rho=0.370, adjusted p<0.001, n=855).

Among these respondents, the link between medical experience and well-being is fairly visible. Healthcare accessibility, whether services are respectful, and economic and family conditions may all affect both.

The questionnaire records medical satisfaction and well-being over the same period; it cannot determine which came first, nor prove that improving medical care directly produces an equal change in well-being.

4.3.2 Overall distribution of medical satisfaction

Satisfaction ratings cluster at lower and middle levelsKey finding

Among respondents who answered the medical-satisfaction question (n=859), very dissatisfied 21.8% (187 people), level 2 32.5% (279 people), level 3 32.1% (276 people), level 4 10.9% (94 people), and very satisfied 2.7% (23 people).

Combining "very dissatisfied" and "level 2", over half (54.2%) hold negative or somewhat negative views of current transgender medical services. Only 13.6% report level 4 or very satisfied. This distribution suggests substantial room for improving medical-service experience.

Reading note: this is an ordered-rating issue; the percentages describe the distribution of rating levels. A mean may be computed as a summary statistic, but ordinal ratings should not be treated as interval measures — respondents may understand "average" or "fairly satisfied" differently.

4.3.3 The dual role of cost and family opposition

Cost and family opposition are the two most common barriersKey finding

As noted, in the medical-barriers question (n=806, multi-select), family not understanding or opposing accounts for 59.9% and cost burden 51.7%. Both exceed half, clearly above other barrier types.

Possible mechanisms / interpretive discussion (not directly measured by this question): family opposition may appear as direct prohibition of medical care, refusal of financial support, blocking minors' guardian consent, or indirect interference through verbal pressure and emotional control. Cost burden covers HRT medication, check-ups, surgery, and transport/accommodation for cross-region care. For young respondents still economically dependent (as in Chapter 2, 18–22 account for 43.5%), family opposition and cost burden may intertwine: even with personal will, family refusal of financial support can block care. These mechanisms draw on community experience and existing research; they are not direct measurements from this question.

Improving medical accessibility therefore requires addressing family knowledge and attitudes, affordability (insurance coverage and low-cost services), and the legal/ethical framework of minors' medical decision rights.

4.3.4 Obtaining a diagnosis certificate

"The largest share want a 'transsexualism' or 'gender dysphoria/gender incongruence' diagnosis certificate but meet difficulties"Key finding

Among respondents who answered the diagnosis-certificate question (n=801 ), want but meet difficulties (e.g. age, cost, family objections) 37.3% (299 people), already obtained 30.3% (243 people), trying to obtain 17.4% (139 people), and not planning to obtain 15.0% (120 people).

About 30% already obtained one, while "want but meet difficulties" (37.3%) is slightly higher. Combining "trying to obtain" and "want but meet difficulties", over half (54.7% ) are in a state of wanting but not yet having. Diagnosis certificates serve practical purposes in some settings (medical processes, document changes), and difficulty obtaining them interweaves with the barriers described earlier (age limits, cost, family objections). Meanwhile, "not planning to obtain" (15.0%) shows not everyone treats the certificate as necessary — some may decline out of privacy concerns, questions about the diagnostic framework, or other reasons.

4.4 HRT health monitoring

Monitoring is insufficient; "want check-ups but lack conditions" is a key gapKey finding

Among respondents who answered the HRT check-up question (n=711), the share with regular check-ups is low.

33.1% (235 people) check occasionally, 28.7% (204 people) want to check but lack conditions, 20.4% (145 people) check regularly, and 17.9% (127 people) have never checked.

Combining "never checked" and "want to but lack conditions", nearly half (46.6%) have unmet monitoring needs. The "want to but lack conditions" category is especially notable: respondents already recognize the importance of monitoring, yet cannot do it due to cost, geographic distance, lack of a trustworthy medical institution, or fear of identity exposure.

The gap between ongoing medication needs and monitoring conditions suggests HRT support should not stop at drug access — check-up accessibility, result interpretation, and referral mechanisms belong in the same service chain. The questionnaire only records monitoring experiences and difficulties; it cannot confirm specific health consequences or risk changes.

Reading note: this question was open only to respondents on a particular HRT path (n=711) and does not represent all HRT users or all respondents. Not checking or checking occasionally does not equal existing health harm, but it does mean fewer opportunities for risk monitoring and early intervention.

4.5 Voice needs and satisfaction

Voice is a prominent source of gender-expression pressure; satisfaction is generally lowKey finding

Difficulty using one's voice: among respondents who answered the voice-use question (n=798), voice causes significant anxiety for many.

"Very hard; my voice is one of my main anxiety sources" 46.2% (369 people), and "impossible" 19.5% (156 people). Together, 65.8% face great difficulty or complete impossibility in using a satisfying voice.

Those dissatisfied with their voice clearly outnumber those satisfiedKey finding

Satisfaction with current voice: among respondents who answered the voice-satisfaction question (n=840), dissatisfaction clearly outweighs satisfaction.

Very dissatisfied 29.9% (251 people), fairly dissatisfied 27.0% (227 people), average 26.3% (221 people), and very satisfied 3.6% (30 people).

Combining "very dissatisfied" and "fairly dissatisfied", over half (56.9% ) hold negative views of their current voice. In contrast, "fairly satisfied" 13.2% (111 people) plus "very satisfied" 3.6% (30 people) total only 16.8%.

The uniqueness of voice needs: voice is not merely an aesthetic preference — it is directly tied to daily expression, exposure concerns, and psychological stress. In phone calls, face-to-face conversations, job interviews, and medical consultations, voice can become a cue that outs a transgender identity, bringing discrimination risk or expression constraints. Voice training and support services (speech therapy, voice feminization/masculinization training, voice-surgery information and referral) should be treated as a standalone need, not an appendix to the medical chapter.

Reading note: the voice-use question (n=798) and the voice-satisfaction question (n=840) have different denominators and measure different dimensions (difficulty versus satisfaction evaluation); percentages are not directly comparable. Voice status should not be pathologized, nor should it be assumed everyone wants a different voice — but the prevalence of voice anxiety in this sample should be recognized.

4.6 Tests with no clear association in these data

The unmet-HRT-need vs. distress association fell short of adjusted significanceKey finding

This analysis found no clear statistical association between "want to use HRT but not yet started" and psychological distress (Spearman rho=-0.070, n=822, adjusted p=0.087).

This does not mean HRT accessibility is unrelated to mental health. Here "unmet HRT need" is simplified to "want but not started", without distinguishing waiting reasons, waiting length, or previous use then stopping; psychological distress is likewise a simplified record in the questionnaire. Because the report tests many relationships, statisticians raise the bar to avoid treating chance differences as real findings. These data did not clear the bar — evidence is not yet clear, not proof of no relationship.

4.7 Chapter summary

This chapter's findings reveal multiple barriers to healthcare and unmet needs:

  1. HRT use and gaps: over 70% are on HRT (71.9%), but 14.6% want to start without having, and 7.6% used and stopped — clear unmet needs.

  2. Channel distribution: among valid respondents to the cross-version-merged HRT-access question (n=716), online private sellers 66.6%; the de-duplicated formal-channel union from cross-recomputation is in 4.2. Domestic platforms/grey cross-border merchants, others' homemade, and homemade products each run 10%–30%, reflecting insufficient formal service access.

  3. Multiple barriers: family opposition (59.9%), cost burden (51.7%), discrimination concerns (40.0%), resource shortage (35.4%), and insufficient professional supply (33.6%). Those more satisfied with medical care also tend to have higher well-being (rho=0.370) — a link, not proof of causation.

  4. Monitoring gaps: 20.4% check regularly; 28.7% want to but lack conditions; 17.9% never checked. A clear gap between ongoing medication needs and monitoring conditions persists.

  5. Voice anxiety: voice is a prominent gender-expression pressure; 65.8% face great difficulty achieving a satisfying voice or cannot at all; 56.9% are dissatisfied with their current voice. Voice support deserves standalone presentation.

Improving transgender healthcare accessibility thus requires simultaneously addressing family support, affordability, regional resource coverage, professional training, privacy protection, and continuity of health monitoring. Voice support should be included in the gender-affirmation support system as an independent service. During the transition period where formal services are not fully covered, harm-reduction information and safe-medication guidance matter equally.

Later chapters present experiences in family, campus, employment, and mental health — domains deeply intertwined with the barriers and costs of healthcare access.

5.1 How the family learned and their initial reactions

Awareness is not support — silence, blame, and non-understanding are commonKey finding

5.1.1 How the family learned

Among respondents who answered the family-awareness question (n=844), the ways families learned are diverse.

Know — I came out voluntarily 36.6% (309 people), don't know 29.6% (250 people), know — passive coming out/passive discovery 20.1% (170 people). Additionally, suspecting but unconfirmed 13.4% (113 people), and the remaining low-frequency categories together 0.2% (2 people).

Voluntary coming out is the largest category (36.6%), but nearly 30% (29.6%) have families who still do not know, and another 20% (20.1%) were learned via passive coming-out or passive discovery.

Possible mechanisms / interpretive discussion (not directly measured by this question): passive coming out may mean respondents had to face family reactions unprepared, or were discovered through external cues (medical records, delivered parcels, social-media leaks). These mechanisms draw on community experience and existing research; they are not direct measurements from this question.

This distribution shows family awareness is a complex process that cannot be reduced to a binary "out or not". Nearly 30% of families not knowing means a substantial share still hide their identity at home — possibly delaying disclosure out of fear of family reactions, economic dependence, or safety risks.

5.1.2 Main reactions after the family found out

Among respondents whose families know (n=486, multi-select), reactions after learning are mainly negative or neutral.

Silence/avoidance 58.2% (283 people), blame/accusation 48.4% (235 people), "don't understand" 47.7% (232 people), and support/acceptance 25.3% (123 people).

Negative reactions (blame/accusation, non-understanding) and passive responses (silence/avoidance) are both clearly higher than support/acceptance (25.3%).

Possible mechanisms / interpretive discussion (not directly measured by this question): silence/avoidance (58.2%) as the most common reaction may reflect family members not knowing how to respond, avoiding conflict, or refusing to acknowledge reality. The high shares of blame/accusation and "don't understand" (both near half) suggest that awareness does not automatically bring support — a substantial share of families show denial or confusion initially. These mechanisms draw on community experience and existing research.

Reading note: this was a multi-select question; the same family may show several reactions at once (e.g. some members support while others blame). Support/acceptance at 25.3% does not mean one quarter of families fully support — it may mean at least one family member expressed support.

5.2 Overall family support and its change

Family support remains limited; some respondents retrospectively report improvement; support relates to well-beingKey finding

5.2.1 Retrospective direction of family attitude change

Among respondents who answered the attitude-change question (n=312), retrospectively reported improvement is the most common direction, but not universal.

Somewhat better 33.3% (104 people), much better 16.0% (50 people), no clear change 36.9% (115 people), much worse 8.7% (27 people), and somewhat worse 5.1% (16 people).

Combining "somewhat better" and "much better", nearly half (49.4%) retrospectively report family attitude improvement. However, over a third (36.9%) report basically no change and 13.8% report deterioration. This is the one question directly asking about change direction, so it is the primary basis for the conclusion here; it remains a retrospective self-report rather than a two-wave tracking measurement.

5.2.2 Snapshot of support right after the family found out

In the support-level question about when the family first learned (n=476), completely unsupportive 37.2% (177 people), neutral or uncertain 25.6% (122 people), little support 23.3% (111 people), more support 10.9% (52 people), and very supportive 2.9% (14 people). Combining "completely unsupportive" and "little support", 60.5% felt no support on that question; "more" and "very" support together 13.9%.

5.2.3 Snapshot of current support level

Among respondents who answered the current family-support question (n=324), completely unsupportive 26.9% (87 people), neutral or uncertain 26.5% (86 people), little support 21.3% (69 people), more support 17.6% (57 people), and very supportive 7.7% (25 people).

"More" and "very" support together 25.3%; the remaining 74.7% sit at little support, neutral, or completely unsupportive.

Reading boundary: the two questions — right-after-learning and current — have different respondent sets (n=476 and n=324); the percentages describe two cross-sectional snapshots and cannot be subtracted into "decline", "increase", or "net change". Conclusions about attitude change rely on the n=312 direct-change question.

Some families improved after learningKey finding

As noted, 49.4% report family attitudes somewhat or much better. This suggests family attitudes can change; continuous, re-entrable family education and support programmes may fit actual needs better than one-time persuasion.

Retrospective reports also show no change or deteriorationKey finding

As noted, 36.9% of respondents report basically no change and 13.8% report deterioration (much worse 8.7%, somewhat worse 5.1%). This shows improvement cannot be assumed for all families; as the questionnaire captures change from a single time point, it cannot determine how long an attitude persisted.

5.2.4 Differences between fathers' and mothers' support

Fathers and mothers differ descriptively in awareness status and support distributionKey finding

Alongside overall family support, the survey further examined support from each parent (mother and father) at the two stages — right after learning and currently.

In the mother-support question for when she first learned (n=308): completely unsupportive 37.3% (115 people), neutral or uncertain 23.1% (71 people), little support 22.7% (70 people), more support 10.4% (32 people), very supportive 4.2% (13 people), and 2.3% (7 people) had not told the mother. In the mother's current-support question (n=305): neutral or uncertain 26.2% (80 people), completely unsupportive 21.6% (66 people), little support 20.0% (61 people), more support 18.0% (55 people), very supportive 9.2% (28 people), and not told 4.9% (15 people).

In the father-support question for when he first learned (n=299): completely unsupportive 43.1% (129 people), neutral or uncertain 16.7% (50 people), little support 16.7% (50 people), not told 16.1% (48 people), more support 6.0% (18 people), and low-frequency/other merged (n<5 each) 1.3% (4 people). In the father's current-support question (n=294): completely unsupportive 29.9% (88 people), neutral or uncertain 19.4% (57 people), not told 17.7% (52 people), little support 15.3% (45 people), more support 11.2% (33 people), and very supportive 6.5% (19 people).

Two descriptive features appear. First, the share of fathers "not told" is descriptively higher than mothers in both stage questions: fathers 16.1% and 17.7%, mothers 2.3% and 4.9%. This report ran no formal paired test on this difference, so only the descriptive difference is reported, without inferring communication causes. Second, mothers' and fathers' support distributions differ across the two questions; but denominators and respondent sets differ, so these percentages cannot be written as individual-level rates or longitudinal change.

5.2.7 Family support, well-being, and identity expression

Those with more family support tend to have higher overall well-being (Spearman rho=0.321, adjusted p<0.001, n=324). Family support and identity-expression status are also statistically associated (Cramér's V=0.170, adjusted p=0.0059, n=316).

Family support and expression status show an adjusted-significant statistical associationKey finding

In this sample, the link between family support and well-being is fairly visible, and people with different family support differ in expression status. Improving family environments has real-world relevance, but these results alone cannot say which side changed first.

Reading note for this subsection: the survey records family support, well-being, and expression at the same time; it cannot prove family support directly causes changes in well-being or expression. Age, economic conditions, regional culture, and family dynamics may also influence these outcomes. 5.3 Attributions of family non-support

Non-support is mainly attributed to knowledge misunderstandings, traditional values, and social pressureKey finding

Among respondents who answered the non-support-reason question (n=462, multi-select), attributions concentrate on knowledge, values, and social pressure. Lack of understanding or misconceptions about transgender people 79.2% (366 people), traditional values (carrying on the family line, gender roles) 78.8% (364 people), worry about social opinion or pressure from relatives and friends 74.2% (343 people), worry about HRT side effects or health risks 71.9% (332 people), and concern about economic burden 27.1% (125 people).

Knowledge misunderstanding is the most cited attribution (79.2%). The high shares of traditional values (78.8%) and social opinion/relative-friend pressure (74.2%) suggest family reactions are shaped not only by individual attitudes but also by cultural norms, social expectations, and external judgment.

Reading note: these data reflect respondents' judgments about family reasons, not a direct survey of family members. Attributions may be influenced by respondents' understanding, family communication styles, and psychological defences. One family may combine several reasons (e.g. knowledge misconceptions plus worries about carrying on the family line).

This suggests family-facing support services need to address knowledge misconceptions (accurate, non-pathologizing information), value conflicts (the balance between traditional values and individual autonomy), and social-pressure concerns (supporting families in dealing with external judgment and privacy protection) at once.

5.4 Family restrictions and violence

Some respondents experience verbal, medical, economic, and personal restrictions at homeKey finding

Among respondents who answered the past-year family restriction/violence question (n=474, multi-select), a share experienced multiple forms of substantive restriction and harm.

Verbal/psychological violence (insults, threats, belittling) 39.7% (188 people), refusal of or interference with medical decisions (e.g. forbidding HRT) 33.3% (158 people), economic violence (survival-level or zero allowance, forced income confiscation) 20.0% (95 people), restricting leaving the home or demanding full-time accompaniment 15.2% (72 people), physical violence (hitting, kicking, shoving) 14.3% (68 people), restricting phone/internet use 12.4% (59 people), confiscating ID documents or bank cards 8.4% (40 people), and forced placement in a "correction" institution 3.0% (14 people).

Verbal/psychological violence is the most common family harm (39.7%), followed by medical interference (33.3%). Economic violence (20.0%), restricting leaving home (15.2%), and physical violence (14.3%) each sit at 10%–20%. More extreme controls — confiscating documents, restricting phone/internet, forced "correction" institutions — are also reported (8.4%, 12.4%, 3.0%).

This distribution shows family harm is not only attitudinal or verbal: it involves medical autonomy (refusing or interfering with HRT), economic control (withholding allowance, forced income surrender), freedom of movement (restricting leaving home, full-time accompaniment), and bodily safety (physical violence). For young respondents still economically dependent, these restrictions can severely impair access to healthcare, education, employment, and social support.

Family restrictions extend to economic, movement, network, and document controlKey finding

As noted: economic violence 20.0%, restricting leaving home or demanding accompaniment 15.2%, restricting phone/internet 12.4%, confiscating ID documents or bank cards 8.4%. These controls may make it hard to seek medical care, education, jobs, or external support independently.

Reading note: this multi-select question touches highly sensitive content and should be presented neutrally, without dramatization. Selecting an option means the respondent experienced it within the past year; not selecting does not mean complete absence (it may be unreported out of privacy concerns, psychological defence, or differing understanding of "violence"). These experiences should not be attributed to transgender identity itself; they can be read within family power dynamics, generational conflict, and social environment, but the questionnaire cannot determine specific causes.

This suggests safety support must go beyond emotional comfort and information provisioning to cover practical resources and action capacity: low-threshold safety planning, legal and psychological referral, emergency economic support, temporary-housing information, and protection mechanisms for minors.

5.4.1 Exploratory comparison: economic independence vs. family support and restrictions/violence

People with different economic-independence levels show some proportional differences in family support and restrictions/violence, but this analysis found no clear statistical association. In the current family-support question (n=292), the family-dependent group (n=219) shows 22.8% completely unsupportive and 27.9% more/very supportive; the independent group (n=54) shows 33.3% and 14.8%. In the family restriction/violence question (n=444), the dependent group (n=332) reports any violence at 57.5%, the independent group (n=85) at 45.9%. Adjusted p-values for economic independence vs. current family support (rho=-0.127, n=292) and the 9 restriction/violence tests all exceed 0.05. Medical interference shows a weak negative association before correction (rho=-0.120, raw p=0.011) but does not reach the adjusted threshold.

These proportional differences warrant further study, but the data are insufficient to confirm stable relationships. Because several restriction/violence experiences were tested together, the statistical bar was raised to avoid mistaking chance differences for real findings.

5.5 Chapter summary

This chapter's findings reveal the complexity of family relationships:

  1. Diverse ways of knowing: 36.6% came out voluntarily; 29.6% of families do not know; 20.1% were passive coming-out/passive discovery. Family awareness is a complex process, not a binary "out or not".

  2. Awareness is not support: after learning, silence/avoidance (58.2%), blame/accusation (48.4%), and non-understanding (47.7%) all exceed support/acceptance (25.3%).

  3. Limited support and inconsistent retrospective change: in the direct-change question (n=312), 49.4% report improvement, 36.9% basically no change, 13.8% deterioration. In the two support snapshots with different respondent sets, complete non-support was 37.2% right after learning (n=476) and 26.9% currently (n=324); no longitudinal subtraction is made. Fathers' "not told" share is descriptively higher than mothers', with no corresponding formal paired test.

  4. Support relates to well-being and expression: those with more family support tend to have higher well-being (rho=0.321); groups differing in family support differ in expression status (Cramér's V=0.170). These results show association, not proof that family support directly causes change.

  5. Attributions of non-support: lack of understanding or misconceptions (79.2%), traditional values (78.8%), and social opinion or relative-friend pressure (74.2%) are the main attributions, suggesting family-facing support must address knowledge, values, and social pressure at once.

  6. Restrictions and violence: 39.7% experienced verbal/psychological violence in the past year, 33.3% medical interference, 20.0% economic violence, 14.3% physical violence. Family harm touches medical autonomy, economic control, freedom of movement, and bodily safety.

Family is both a potentially important protective factor and a source of pressure and risk. Support strategies should include: accurate family-facing knowledge, conflict de-escalation and long-term education; safety planning, legal and psychological referral, and emergency economic support for respondents; and for minors, protection mechanisms and discussion of the legal/ethical framework of medical decision rights.

Later chapters present campus, employment, mental health, and public-service experiences — domains interwoven with family environment to form respondents' living conditions.

Reading note: these data rest on subjective attribution and cannot prove that transgender identity directly "causes" breaks or dropout. Over 40% (44.0%) attend schools with no relevant policy; only 5.6% attend schools with explicit, trans-friendly policies. 6.3 Chapter summary

This chapter presents respondents' reports of campus negative experiences, support, and policy gaps:

  1. Widespread negative experiences: 73.7% report at least one clear negative experience; verbal discrimination/ridicule (49.3%), isolation by classmates (44.6%), required dress codes (36.0%), and physical harassment/violence (27.2%) are the most common. More negative campus experiences correlate with more distress (rho=0.149).

  2. Scarce support: over 70% sit at almost no support or only sporadic support; overall supportive schools are under 20% (19.4%). More school support relates to higher well-being (rho=0.278).

  3. Policy gaps: over 40% attend schools with no relevant policy; explicit, effectively implemented gender-diversity policies are extremely rare (5.6%). Generic anti-bullying policies often omit gender-identity protection.

  4. Empty policies: policy existence is not effective protection; 8.0% report hollow policies, highlighting the need to address policy content, enforcement mechanisms, and complaint channels together.

  5. Educational interruption: 26.6% attribute breaks/dropout to their transgender identity (direct 13.6% + partial 13.0%); this subjective attribution deserves follow-up research.

Improving campus conditions for transgender students requires: explicit inclusion of gender-identity and expression protection in anti-bullying policies; support mechanisms with accountable staff, confidential procedures, and complaint channels; professional training for teachers; and converting individual goodwill into enforceable, accountable institutions. School support must not depend on individual teachers' kindness — it needs systemic policy support.

  1. Concealment is the main cost: 52.1% must conceal their identity because it is not disclosed; 36.7% must maintain expression inconsistent with their gender identity. Sustained concealment and inconsistent expression are themselves the most common workplace burdens.

  2. Documents and rejection: 23.2% were questioned because documents mismatch appearance; 21.3% were rejected for a job due to gender expression. Document systems directly intersect employment experience.

  3. Negative economic impact: 50.5% believe their transgender identity negatively affected finances; positive impact is extremely low (4.9%).

  4. No clear association found: this data shows no clear relationship between expression and negative employment experiences (adjusted p=0.889), but the absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Sample size, simplified measurement, and multiple employment factors may affect the result.

Improving transgender employment environments requires: explicit anti-discrimination policies and complaint mechanisms; inclusive redesign of recruitment, dress, name use, and document-verification processes; and support services for the psychological costs of concealment and inconsistent expression. Beyond overt discrimination, sustained concealment and inconsistent expression are themselves significant burdens in the workplace and need to be visible in policy design and service provision.

8.5 Chapter summary

This chapter's findings reveal a complex picture of mental health and well-being:

  1. Widespread distress: nearly 90% experienced at least one high-frequency emotional distress in the past six months; frequent anxiety (61.8%), frequent depressive moods (61.1%), and emotional turbulence (58.0%) are the most common.

  2. Multi-layered environmental pressure: sources include gender identity/body anxiety (83.7%), schoolwork (59.6%), family (58.6%), finances (56.7%), public policy/social opinion (41.4%), and medical access (32.9%). Distress cannot be explained apart from external environments.

  3. Support access difficulties: 45.5% find psychological support hard to access, clearly above those who find it easy (23.0%).

  4. Fairly frequent motivation decline: 43.0% fairly frequently reported reduced life motivation (almost always or often) in the past six months — support should not be limited to acute crisis intervention.

  5. Self-harm and suicide-related experiences: 68.2% report a self-harm history; 88.9% reported at least one suicide-related category . These are evidence of safety support needs, not identity danger, and should not be attributed to transgender identity.

  6. Well-being distribution: 47.1% hold negative views of overall well-being; only 20.7% report fairly or very happy. Well-being is statistically associated with identity expression, family support, medical satisfaction, school support, and support-source count.

Mental health support therefore requires: trauma-informed, non-pathologizing services; low-threshold crisis support and long-term psychological services; simultaneous handling of family, educational, economic, and medical barriers; and harm-reduction-oriented, safety-planning, and referral mechanisms for self-harm and suicide-related experiences. Support strategies should not focus only on individual psychological intervention — external environmental conditions need improvement too.

9.4 Chapter summary

This chapter presents respondents' reported document, facility, and everyday-environment barriers:

  1. Documents and public affairs: nearly half of relevant respondents (48.8%) at least occasionally encountered questioning or inappropriate treatment in public affairs in the past six months. Document difficulties and public-service difficulties are statistically associated (Cramér's V=0.173).

  2. Public facility use: only 14.7% can comfortably use identity-matching public facilities. Avoidance (22.9%) and alternatives (25.8%) are common coping strategies, indicating demand for gender-neutral public facilities.

Public-life barriers thus involve three layers: document systems, public facility design, and the social environment. Improvement paths include: simplified, accessible document change; reformed front-desk identity-verification processes; gender-neutral public facility supply; and inclusive education for society.

While respecting individual autonomy, action recommendations should respond to the diverse needs expressed, not make a single medical path the only exit.

Combining findings from Chapters 2 to 10, the survey presents five interwoven threads:

Thread 1: Young and diverse sample, early awareness, severely constrained everyday expression

The sample is dominated by respondents aged 18–22 (43.5%), and gender identities are diverse. More than 80% began noticing their gender identity difference at or before age 17. Yet the share able to live fully as their gender identity is not high (16.8%); expression is heavily concentrated online (87.7%) and in trusted friend circles (55.3%), while formal settings — family, school, healthcare, employment — are clearly lower.

Implication: gender awareness emerges in a life stage where family and school still heavily shape daily life, but formal settings lack conditions for safe expression. Support systems need both age-appropriateness and setting-specific targeting.

Thread 2: Interwoven real barriers across healthcare, family, campus, employment, documents, and public space

  • Healthcare: HRT access relies heavily on informal channels (online private sellers 66.6%); barriers include family opposition (59.9%), cost (51.7%), discrimination concerns, and resource shortage.
  • Family: awareness is not support; silence, blame, and non-understanding are common; some respondents experience verbal, medical, economic, and personal restrictions.
  • Campus: 73.7% report negative campus experiences; school policies explicitly covering gender diversity are extremely rare (5.6%).
  • Employment: concealment (52.1%) and maintaining inconsistent expression (36.7%) are the main costs; 50.5% believe their transgender identity negatively affected their finances.
  • Public space: only 14.7% can comfortably use identity-matching public facilities; document difficulties accompany public-service difficulties.

Implication: these barriers are not isolated; they are reported across domains at once. For example, family opposition appears alongside healthcare access, economic support, and identity-expression barriers; document-mismatch difficulties likewise appear across employment, public affairs, and public facilities. Action requires cross-departmental, systemic collaboration.

Thread 3: Distress must be interpreted within multi-layered external pressures, not attributed to identity itself

Nearly 90% experienced at least one high-frequency distress in the past six months; pressure sources include gender identity/body anxiety (83.7%), schoolwork (59.6%), family (58.6%), finances (56.7%), public policy/social opinion (41.4%), and medical access (32.9%). Self-harm (68.2%) and suicide-related experiences (88.9%) are common in this sample, and 45.5% find psychological support hard to access.

Implication: distress runs parallel to external environmental pressure, insufficient support, and safety needs; cross-sectional data cannot confirm causal direction, and these experiences are not evidence of transgender-identity danger. Mental health support should be trauma-informed and non-pathologizing, responding at once to family, educational, economic, and medical barriers.

Thread 4: Inner resilience and relational networks protect, but coverage is uneven

The main protective sources are personal inner strength (59.9%) and transgender-community friends (49.4%), while family support is limited in coverage (11.6%). Diverse support sources correlate positively with well-being, but 12.7% still report no current strength or support.

Implication: protective factors include personal resources as well as peer, partner, and community connections. However, structural responsibility should not be shifted onto individual resilience — uneven network coverage means services must proactively reach groups in extreme support scarcity.

Thread 5: Desire for change spans body, voice, finances, psychology, law, and social environment

83.7% want body changes, but desire for voice (68.3%), finances (65.3%), mental health (63.5%), legal documents (55.6%), and family relationships (50.2%) is equally common. 80.0% express a strong desire for change.

Implication: the need for change is not one medical issue but a combination of body, financial, psychological, legal, and social-environmental dimensions. Action recommendations should respond to this diversity.

11.2 Directions for action

11.2.1 Medical services
  • Expand regular, affordable HRT assessment, prescription, and follow-up services, reducing reliance on informal channels.
  • Integrate HRT health monitoring into the service chain, offering affordable, bookable, privacy-protecting check-ups and referral.
  • Provide harm-reduction information during the transition period where formal services do not yet cover, helping informal-channel users lower risk.
  • Treat voice support as a standalone service: informed-consent, non-conversion-based voice training and professional referral.
  • Improve privacy protection and professional training in medical services, reducing the barrier of discrimination concerns to care-seeking.
  • Review potential accessibility barriers related to age and guardian-consent requirements, and explore institutional paths balancing individual autonomy, informed consent, and minor protection (see 4.3.1: bottom/genital reconstruction 60.3%, facial surgery 54.9%; diagnosis certificate "want but meet difficulties" 37.3%).
11.2.2 Family support
  • Provide long-term, re-entrable family education and support programmes rather than one-time persuasion.
  • Offer families accurate, non-pathologizing information that responds to knowledge misconceptions, traditional values, and social pressure.
  • Build low-threshold safety plans, legal and psychological referral, and emergency economic support responding to family restrictions or violence.
11.2.3 Schools
  • Explicitly include protection of gender identity and expression in anti-bullying policies, rather than relying on generic policies.
  • Establish support mechanisms with accountable staff, confidential procedures, and complaint channels, converting individual goodwill into enforceable policy.
  • Provide professional training for teachers, reducing cases where educators become a source of pressure.
  • Gradually reduce social stereotypes through systematic gender education: bring gender-diversity knowledge into curricula, class meetings, and campus outreach, so stereotypes and verbal bias are no longer taken for granted.
  • Promote gender education for students and families, helping them understand the diversity of gender identity and expression and respond to family and community misconceptions.
11.2.4 Employment and economy
  • Drive inclusive redesign of recruitment, dress codes, document verification, name use, and anti-harassment processes.
  • Offer more flexible, privacy-respecting alternatives in identity-verification processes.
11.2.5 Mental health and safety support
  • Provide trauma-informed, non-pathologizing psychological services covering multiple distress types, not a single diagnosis.
  • Build low-threshold crisis support and long-term psychological services covering those with historical, current, and no experience.

11.3 Research limitations

All findings are constrained by the limitations below; readers should consider them carefully when interpreting and applying:

Non-probability sampling and young sample restrict generalisation
Respondents were recruited voluntarily through online channels; the sample is dominated by young respondents (18–22: 43.5%). The results describe only the respondents of this survey and cannot be generalised to all transgender and gender-diverse people in China.
Self-report and cross-sectional design limit interpretation
All data are self-reported and collected at a single time point. All "associations" or "correlations" are statistical and cannot establish temporal order or causal direction; synonymous options across questionnaire versions were merged under a unified scope.
An unexamined item is not "no association"; an item short of adjusted significance is not "no relationship"
The pre-specified tests of F024 (identity expression and negative campus experiences), F025 (expression and negative employment experiences), F026 (unmet HRT need and distress), and F058 (friend/community single-item proxies and well-being) all fell short of adjusted significance. These results should not be read as "no association" — they may be limited by sample size, measurement, or analysis methods.
Passing technical QA does not establish representativeness, validity, external validity, or scientific conclusions
The report's data went through technical quality checks (denominators, missing values, Result_ID tracking), but technical QA only verifies the accuracy of numeric processing — not sample representativeness, measurement validity, or the general scientific applicability of the conclusions.
Reporting bias on sensitive topics
Items on domestic violence, self-harm, and suicide-related experiences may be under- or over-reported; choosing "none", "never", or "no clear negative experience" cannot be inferred as complete absence.
Measurement limits of single items or multi-select proxies
Some core concepts (e.g. "family support", "school support", "well-being", "community support") are measured with single-item ordinal ratings or multi-select proxies that cannot capture every dimension of the concept.
Interpretation limits of multi-select questions
Percentages of multi-select items may sum over 100% and cannot be added into an overall share. Different questions have different valid-respondent denominators, so percentages cannot be directly compared across questions.

11.4 Future research directions

01
Longitudinal tracking studies: collect data over multiple time points to explore temporal order and possible causal pathways among identity expression, family support, medical access, and mental health.
02
Finer measurement instruments: use validated standardized scales for mental health, well-being, and social support to improve measurement validity.
03
Subgroup analyses: with larger samples, stratify by gender identity, age, region, and economic conditions to understand differentiated experiences across subgroups.

11.5 Closing

This survey depicts the situation of respondents in identity awareness, expression, healthcare, family, campus, employment, mental health, public services, and social support. The findings reveal multi-layered interwoven real barriers, alongside individual resilience, community connection, and a clear desire for change.

Once more: all findings describe only the respondents of this survey and cannot be generalised; all statistical associations do not imply causation; distress should be understood within multi-layered external pressures, not attributed to transgender identity itself.

The value of this report lies in grounding service design, policy discussion, and follow-up research in respondents' real experiences as an empirical starting point. Improving the situation of transgender and gender-diverse people requires systemic collaboration across healthcare, family, education, employment, law, and social environment — and respect for each individual's autonomy and diverse needs.
